title: Brand the agent host URI namespaces and convert the project root at the boundary
body:
Names the two URI namespaces in the type system and closes one gap in the conversion point that already exists.

## What the investigation found

The framing that there is no single conversion point turned out to be wrong. `EditorRemoteAgentHostTransport` is that point for the dev-container path, and the local sessions provider deliberately does no mapping of its own precisely so the transport owns it. The real defect is that the transport's field coverage is hand-maintained and silently incomplete, and its map callback was a symmetric string to string, so a call site could pick the wrong direction with no compile error.

Concretely, the transport converted exactly two fields: the working directories array and the folder-picker primary. Anything it does not name stays host-native and is then wrapped by the protocol client into a third namespace. So `project.uri` and `workingDirectories` from the same session object arrived in different namespaces, which is why a comparison between them silently returns false rather than failing.

## What this changes

Two commits.

The first is type-only: the host and client directory namespaces become branded strings, following the existing branded-value precedent in the codebase, and the two directions are named once as fields so a call site cannot pick the wrong one. There are exactly two casts, both at the conversion functions, which is the boundary assertion. Three deliberate breakages were compiled to prove the brand actually rejects a wrong assignment: swapping either direction, or passing the raw value through, each produces a type error rather than silently working.

The second adds `project.uri` to the same single mapping point every carrier of that field already flows through. No action mutates `project`, so those carriers are the complete set, which is what makes this single-point rather than another per-call-site patch. It is safe because the value is host-owned and only ever originates from the other end of this connection, so there is no cross-authority ambiguity. The session list's containment guard is widened alongside, since it admitted only host-native values and would otherwise have excluded exactly the roots that now match.

## What is deliberately not here

The remaining cross-namespace comparisons each need a decision rather than a mapping, and they are enumerated in the branch's investigation. The highest-value one is that the transport's inbound conversion, added in #333296, handles notifications and responses but not incoming requests, which is why auto-approval containment fails: an approved directory in the window's namespace never covers a host-native read. That is a coherent next increment on the same single point and would fix containment, resource-read logging and the plugin read path together.

Two are deliberately excluded rather than deferred. Normalising the multi-root workspace-file provenance would let two different containers' workspace files with the same path compare equal, weakening an identity check that is strict on purpose; that needs an authority-aware comparison, not a mapping. File-edit URIs need a protocol-level decision about whether edits are addressed in host or client space.

Branding the underlying conversion helpers themselves would touch 53 call sites and should wait until that number comes down.

## Tests

Removing the single `project` mapping line fails 6 of 15 transport tests; reverting the store guard fails exactly the remote-namespace test and nothing else. Transport 15 passing, a new store suite at 4, the agent host platform suites at 6192 passing, the agent host services at 82, and the chat agent-sessions browser suite at 1338, all with zero failures. No new type errors.

Part of #333174.

title: agentHost: add MCP connector discovery
body:
## Summary

- add a shared Agent Host service that fetches the product-configured Copilot Connectors `/plugins/connected` catalog with the existing GitHub OAuth credential
- revalidate JSON responses with opaque ETags, apply cache metadata from `304` responses, honor `Cache-Control: no-store`, accept only HTTPS MCP endpoints, and invalidate safely on token changes
- merge connected connector MCP servers into Copilot, Claude, and Codex while preserving user, workspace, and plugin configuration precedence and revalidating stale catalogs in the background at most once per minute
- use the common Agent Host bootstrap so local and remote/server hosts share the same implementation without new AHP token plumbing

## Scope

This draft consumes already-connected connector MCP servers. It does not yet add the catalog/consent UI, PUT/DELETE connection lifecycle, exact-resource OAuth, vendor recovery handling for JSON-RPC codes 1001-1007, or full plugin tarball components.

GHES discovery is intentionally disabled for the current dotcom preview endpoint so an enterprise token is never sent to `api.github.com`.

Issue association: pending; no unambiguous VS Code tracker was found.

## Follow-ups before OAuth scope enforcement

Connector requests will require `write:plugin_gateway_connections` for managing connections and making MCP calls, or `read:plugin_gateway_connections` for read-only access. Existing GitHub OAuth sessions cannot gain either scope without user reauthorization.

GitHub OAuth scope bundles are intentionally aligned across VS Code and integrated extensions so multiple experiences can reuse one authentication session. Because the GitHub authentication provider identifies sessions by their requested scope set, independently adding a connector scope could instead create a parallel session and cause different experiences to request authorization separately.

Before scope enforcement, choose and coordinate one authentication model across affected clients:

- **Additive connector session:** request a connector-capable session only when a user enables or uses connectors. This limits the additional permission and avoids reauthorizing users who do not use connectors, but the extra session, token lifecycle, account selection, and authorization step become intentional product behavior.
- **Shared scope bundle:** add the connector scope to the canonical GitHub scope bundle used by all participating clients. This preserves a single shared session after migration, but requires a coordinated rollout and reauthorization of existing users, including potentially users who do not use connectors.

No individual client should independently change its default GitHub scope bundle without accounting for the other consumers of that shared session.

The following UX and recovery requirements apply under either model:

- show a nonblocking **Update Authorization** action in the connector management surface, including the account and GitHub host whose authorization will be updated
- also surface **Update Authorization** inline when a connector tool call reports insufficient scope, so users do not have to discover the management surface first
- reuse VS Code's existing GitHub authentication provider and setup flow rather than implementing a connector-specific browser or device-code flow
- ensure reauthorization targets the intended existing account; cancellation must leave the current authorization intact
- after authorization succeeds, forward the connector-capable token, refresh the connector catalog and authorization state, update already-running connector sessions, and retry the blocked operation where possible
- distinguish insufficient-scope responses from ordinary catalog failures so enforcement results in an actionable prompt rather than connectors silently disappearing
- add enforcement-mode coverage once the service's insufficient-scope response and challenge contract is finalized; the current live smoke test runs while scope checks are not enforced

## Manual Work IQ Mail smoke test

Prerequisites: use an account with Copilot Connectors preview access and an Outlook mailbox that can consent to Work IQ Mail.

1. Confirm the connector catalog is available:

   ```bash
   PREFIX="copilot-connectors/api/v1"
   CONNECTOR="a365outlookmailmcp"

   gh api "$PREFIX/plugins" \
     --jq ".plugins[] | select(.name == \"$CONNECTOR\") | {name, status: .connection.status}"
   ```

2. If its status is not `connected`, start the idempotent consent flow and finish it in the browser:

   ```bash
   consent_link=$(gh api -X PUT "$PREFIX/connectors/managed/$CONNECTOR/connection" \
     -f client_source=VS_CODE \
     --jq '.consent_link // empty')
   test -n "$consent_link" && open "$consent_link"
   ```

3. Verify that the callback completed and the canonical connected-plugin endpoint advertises the MCP server:

   ```bash
   gh api "$PREFIX/plugins/connected" \
     --jq ".plugins[] | select(.name == \"$CONNECTOR\") | {name, status: .connection.status, servers: .mcpServers.mcpServers}"
   ```

4. Build and launch the Agents window using the `Run and Compile Agents - OSS` task. Sign in to the same GitHub account, choose **Local**, select **Copilot**, and choose a workspace.

5. Start a fresh session with this read-only prompt:

   > Use the Work IQ Mail MCP tools to list my 5 most recent email messages. Show only sender, received time, and subject. Do not send, delete, move, mark, archive, or otherwise modify anything.

6. Approve `a365outlookmailmcp-SearchMessagesQueryParameters` for the session. If the result exceeds the inline tool-output limit, also approve reading the generated temporary `copilot-tool-output-*.txt` file.

Expected result:

- the Customizations area includes `a365outlookmailmcp`
- the connector search tool completes and the response lists five messages
- no mail is modified
- `agenthost.log` contains connector activity with no `AgentHostMcpConnectorsService` warning or connector authorization error

Verified locally on 2026-09-03 against the live preview: the end-to-end Copilot turn completed successfully in 46 seconds with zero connector errors.

## Testing

- `npm run typecheck-client`
- targeted ESLint for all PR-owned TypeScript files
- connector service contract tests: 11 passing
- merged service graph and Codex fixture suites: 178 passing
- merged Copilot, Claude, and Codex MCP-focused tests: 29 passing
- live Work IQ Mail test described above

title: Hydrate replay attribution into a resumed session
body:
Hydrates the replay attribution index into a resumed session, so a tool result that arrives after a restart is attributed to the turn it belongs to instead of being dropped as unknown or misfiled onto the live turn.

**Stacked on #334047**, which exposes the index and the resolver but deliberately wires nothing to a live session. The commit list below therefore includes it. Draft until that lands; rebasing afterwards leaves only this commit.

## What it does

On resume the session reads the transcript once, builds the attribution seed and hands the pipeline a promise. The router awaits it once at the top of its handle path and hydrates before mapping anything. That seam works because the router's handle is already awaited serially by the consumer loop, and the router already owns the mapper state and the subagent registry the seed populates.

The seed gets its own read rather than reusing the restore's. The restore read is driven by the renderer asking for a transcript, so it can run before the session exists, after it, or never, and it is not sequenced against materialize. Hydration is kicked off unawaited, since the consumer loop does not start until the first send, which every caller issues after materialize resolves; awaiting it would put a transcript read and a full replay pass on the critical path of the first send after a resume.

The mapper then consults it. A tool result whose entry is hydrated and belongs to a different turn than the one in flight is logged with its committed turn, dropped from the registry along with its cached file edit, and emits nothing, because the reducer only mutates the active turn and side effects drop actions aimed at another. Live entries are untouched, so a steer still completes on its own turn, and an unknown id still warns exactly as before.

Two supporting pieces: a rebind now drains the aborted turn's attribution, since abort never delivers a result and that cleanup otherwise never runs and mislabels the next turn's end; and a replayed user envelope is skipped before any attribution, using the SDK's own required replay discriminator rather than a guess.

Hydration failure is swallowed and logged, so a bad transcript degrades to today's behaviour rather than killing the turn.

## Tests

- a resumed session hydrates replay attribution
- a hydrated tool result for a committed turn attributes there and emits nothing
- a replayed user envelope re-attributes nothing
- a rebind drains the aborted turn's attribution
- a control: a hydrated entry whose turn is the in-flight turn still completes

Four of the five fail without the change; the control passes either way, which is its point. 380 passing across the six affected suites, and 4402 passing across the whole agent-host node suite. No new type errors, nothing under the synced protocol directory touched.

## Known ceiling and what is left out

Hydrated entries survive until the first turn boundary, matching the existing drain semantics. A late result arriving in the resumed session's second turn still falls back to the unknown-id warning. That is worth revisiting if results turn out to arrive that late.

The file-edit observer still runs on replayed envelopes; gating it collides with other work in flight, so it is flagged rather than fixed here.

Expect one small conflict with #334008, which adds the same drain method at the same anchor. The bodies are identical; only a doc line differs, and after the merge there are genuinely two call sites, at the rebind and at the final result.

Part of #333174.

title: agentHost: preserve static MCP OAuth client IDs
body:
Supersedes #328347.

## Problem

Agent Host reconstructs workspace and plugin MCP server configuration before handing it to the Copilot SDK. The current path:

- drops nested `oauth.clientId` and SDK-style `oauthClientId` during workspace normalization;
- omits the static OAuth client ID from `toSdkMcpServer`; and
- drops an ID-only `staticClientConfig` unless `publicClient` is explicitly `true`.

For servers such as Slack that require a pre-registered client and do not support Dynamic Client Registration, the runtime consequently receives no client ID. VS Code falls back to DCR and prompts the user to manually provide client registration details.

## Fix

- Normalize both supported workspace client-ID shapes into the internal `oauth.clientId` representation.
- Project the internal client ID to the SDK as `oauthClientId`.
- Preserve ID-only static clients when `publicClient` is omitted, matching the runtime public-client default.
- Let a supplied `clientSecret` take priority over `publicClient`, and cover that behavior with a regression test requested on #328347.

## Validation

- `./scripts/test.sh --grep "pluginParsers|copilotPluginConverters"` (99 passing)

title: Surface sandbox model fallbacks and honour confirmation editability
body:
Three follow-ups to #333897 and #333883, found while re-reviewing both against the agent host protocol. They are independent and can be reviewed in any order.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Part of this intentionally reverts #333897** — see "2. Context tier" below. That deletion is the point of the change, not an accident. Flagging it so it isn't reported as a regression.

### 1. A sandbox turn silently ran on a model the user did not pick

`_carryModelToSandbox` has three paths that give up on the user's selection: no model target, the model isn't advertised, or the catalog doesn't arrive within the wait. All three logged and then dispatched the turn **with no model at all**.

An absent `model` on the message means the agent decides — for a session that has never run, that is its default. So the turn ran at a capability and a price the user hadn't chosen, and because that is a legitimate protocol state, nothing downstream had any reason to report it.

Each path now tells the user which model was dropped. Still a fallback rather than a hard failure: a sandbox has already been provisioned by this point, and failing the send would strand it.

### 2. Context tier was hidden whenever the workbench couldn't decorate it

**This partially reverts #333897.** That change labelled a host's `contextTier` values with token counts (`264K` / `1M`) taken from the workbench's own model catalogue, and dropped the property entirely when it couldn't find them.

Two problems:

- **The labels were paired by array position.** The host's tier enum and the catalogue's context-size list are independent sources. Nothing guarantees they are the same length or the same order, so the pairing mislabels as soon as either changes — showing the user a specific, wrong number.
- **Absent decoration was treated as absent capability.** A host advertises an option because it will honour it. A model the workbench doesn't know, a staged rollout, and a catalogue that hasn't resolved yet are indistinguishable here, and all three silently removed a control the session actually supports.

The host's own labels (`Default` / `Long context`) are now used. This is a deliberate downgrade in label quality — real token counts should come from the host describing its own tiers, not from a client-side join.

### 3. Confirmations invited edits that were thrown away

A tool confirmation renders its input in an editor and writes changes back. Two separate paths do this, and both are affected:

- **Generic input** — `rawInput` is written back, and `ILanguageModelToolsService` assigns it to the tool's parameters after confirmation.
- **Terminal** — the command line is written back to `commandLine.userEdited`, which only the built-in terminal tool reads when it runs the command.

Agent-host confirmations reach neither. They confirm through the protocol, which *does* define a field for an edited input — but nothing in the workbench populates it. So a user could edit a shell command they were approving and watch the original one run.

Adds an optional `editable` flag to both invocation-data shapes:

- **omitted → editable**, so every existing caller is unchanged;
- agent-host confirmations set `false`, and the write-back handler isn't attached at all.

The terminal case sits alongside the existing `presentationOverrides` read-only rule rather than replacing it.

The adapter hardcodes `false` rather than forwarding the protocol's own `editable`, because forwarding a `true` would recreate the exact bug until the edited-input round trip is implemented. Noted in a comment and pinned by tests.

## Testing

`npm run typecheck-client` clean. 3,765 chat tests pass.

New: two tests for the unavailable-model and timeout notifications; two for context-tier labelling and retention; one asserting a generic confirmation is read-only, and one for the terminal confirmation.

One existing assertion in `stateToProgressAdapter.test.ts` updated for the new `editable: false` — it failed first, which is the test doing its job.

## Not verified

No UI run. The read-only editors and the notification are covered by unit tests and by reading the render paths, **not by observation**. The 5-second model wait is unchanged and still unvalidated — this only makes its expiry visible.

## Not included

- Removing the permission-metadata fallback from #333883. Still in the wrong layer, but its replacement doesn't exist yet, so removing it now would regress shipped behaviour. Documented in place with the condition for deleting it.
- Removing the model catalogue join. Its token-limit half is a shim that a host can make dead by populating native protocol fields; its pricing half is not, because pricing is deliberately kept off the protocol as operator-sensitive. Dropping the join therefore means dropping pricing for these models — a product decision rather than a cleanup. The comment now separates the two.
- Implementing the edited-input round trip.

title: Keep a primed subagent spawn alive past the next turn
body:
Keeps a subagent spawn that was primed from the transcript alive past the next turn, so a restored subagent's identity survives and a background subagent that outlived a host restart can still complete.

## Defect

`SubagentRegistry` doubles as the agent-id cache the subagent transcript resolver reads, and `primeFromTranscript` fills it on resume. Those records were written through `recordSpawn`, so they looked like ordinary in-flight foreground spawns, and `drainForegroundSpawns` removed every one of them at the end of the next turn while warning that a pending spawn had been abandoned.

Two consequences. The resolver's warm cache is destroyed one turn after priming, so reopening a restored subagent chat re-runs the whole strategy chain. More seriously, a background subagent that outlived a host restart has no task-started event in the resumed stream to mark it as background, so its record is drained too, and the later task notification finds no spawn to complete.

A live foreground spawn is already removed on its own tool result, so the drain was catching almost nothing else.

## Fix

A spawn records whether it is actually in flight. The drain now takes only in-flight foreground spawns, and priming records an agent id without claiming the spawn is running.

## Tests

- `drainForegroundSpawns keeps agentId-only records, so a spawn primed from the transcript survives the first resumed turn`, driving the real priming path
- `a background subagent known only from the transcript still completes after a turn ends`, driving the mapper with a result followed by a task notification

Reverting the gate fails both; the second is the substantive one, producing no completion signal at all. 586 passing across the Claude agent, subagent signals, mapper, side effects, registry, resolver, router and replay suites. No new type errors.

## Scope

This does not touch the message router. Two open PRs already cover the messages that arrive while no turn is in flight: #331872 routes the background subagent's system notification, and #332075 maps resumed output under the spawn's turn. This change is what makes the spawn still be there when those messages arrive.

Its visible payoff for the restart case is gated on a separate gap: the restore path never creates a subagent chat entry, so the completion this restores currently has nowhere to land. The fix is correct and prerequisite either way, and the registry and mapper behaviour is asserted directly.

Part of #333174.

title: Surface Copilot tool progress instead of discarding it
body:
Routes Copilot's tool progress to the tool's progress line instead of discarding it, matching what #334053 does for Codex.

**Stacked on #334053.** That PR owns the shared plumbing, the `progressMessage` meta key and the workbench adapter hook, so this branch is based on it rather than on main. The commit list below therefore includes its two commits. This is a draft until it lands; rebasing onto main afterwards leaves only the Copilot commit.

## The gap

Copilot receives `tool.execution_progress` and only trace-logs it, so the status a tool reports while running is discarded. Codex had the opposite problem, merging progress into the tool's output, which #334053 fixes by routing it through `_meta.progressMessage`. This gives Copilot the same route.

## The payload is the same concept

Worth stating, since it decides the treatment. The SDK declares `ToolExecutionProgressData` as `progressMessage: string`, documented as a human-readable status message from an MCP server, plus the tool call id. No percentage, no structured payload, no textless heartbeat. It is the same MCP progress notification Codex maps, so nothing had to be forced into a message field.

## The change

The session tracks whether each tool call is Running and what progress it last sent, then emits `ChatToolCallContentChanged` carrying the message in `_meta` with the content left untouched, routed through the parent tool call id for a subagent. Repeats are coalesced.

The Running flag mirrors the reducer's own transitions and is maintained in the single funnel every emitted action passes through, so it cannot drift as emission sites are added. The gate matters: the reducer ignores a content-changed action unless the call is Running, so a message emitted while the call is paused awaiting authentication would be dropped by the reducer yet still recorded as last sent, and a later valid repeat would then be coalesced away and never shown. The reducer also replaces the whole meta bag, so the start-time meta is re-spread, following the existing convention in this file.

## Progress is not partial output

Distinguished by what the payload is, not by tool name. `tool.execution_partial_result` carries the tool's real stdout as cumulative snapshots: it is gated on shell tools, appended to a terminal resource and to the call's content, and reaches the result. `tool.execution_progress` carries a transient status line that never touches content and lives only in meta. The partial-result path is untouched, and a test asserts a shell tool interleaving both keeps its terminal channel and content identical while the progress action rides alongside carrying only meta.

## The workbench needed no change

The adapter reads the meta key off any Running tool call and never inspects scheme, tool name or contributor, and Copilot's action flows through the identical reducer path. This commit touches no workbench file, which confirms #334053's adapter work is genuinely provider-agnostic rather than Codex-specific.

## Tests

A progress event travels as meta without altering content, identical repeats are coalesced, progress after completion is dropped, and the partial-result terminal channel is unaffected. Three of the four fail without the change; the fourth is an absence assertion that passes either way by design.

`copilotAgentSession` 417 passing, `copilotAgent` 335 passing, `agentMetaReaders` 32 passing. No new type errors.

title: Close abandoned turns deterministically
body:
Closes a turn whose producer has gone, deterministically and with no timers, and fixes two leaks that were creating abandoned turns in the first place.

## Why

Nothing ever ends a turn once the thing that should have ended it is gone. Every stranded-turn symptom shares this root: a tool stuck Running forever, a response that spins indefinitely, steering silently refused because there is no in-flight turn, queued messages never admitted, and a session that can never be released because it still looks busy. The only existing watchdog is telemetry, which reports a hung turn and dispatches nothing.

## What closes a turn

One deterministic rule, no wall clock. After `sendMessage` resolves, if the turn it sent is still the active turn, its completion was dropped, because for a provider whose call settles with the turn the terminal signal is dispatched before that promise's continuation runs. Such a turn is completed when the provider reports its call resolved, or failed as non-resumable `executionAbandoned` when it reports rejected or never started.

This is gated on a new provider-declared `callSettlesWithTurn`, not inferred. Copilot's `send` resolves with a message id and its turn ends later on idle, and Codex resolves early too, so a snapshot-only gate would have closed live turns for both on nearly every send. Only the Claude pipeline sets the flag. There is a regression test for a provider whose send returns before its turn ends.

A turn is never closed while anything is legitimately waiting: a request the provider still tracks, or one the user can see in state as an unanswered input request or a tool call pending confirmation, result confirmation or authentication. `quietMs` is collected in the snapshot and deliberately read by nothing.

## Two leaks that created abandoned turns

- A stale tool ready was dropped without answering, leaking the SDK's permission callback for any tool that reached a terminal state before its ask arrived. It is now denied.
- Removing an active client left that client's parked client-tool calls waiting forever. They are now failed. This required tagging each parked call with its owning client, resolved through the existing owner lookup.

## Supporting work

Claude now implements the existing `IAgent.getTurnDiagnosticSnapshot` seam that Copilot already implemented and Claude reported as unsupported: the prompt queue can say whether a turn is still queued or yielded, the pipeline records each turn as resolved or rejected and derives session state from its rebind and disposal flags, and the session appends the ids currently parked in its permission, user-input and client-tool registries. Both synthesized-terminal sites now route through one `_endTurnFromHost` helper that guards the turn is still active and not already cancelled, so a user cancel racing the close ends the turn exactly once.

One ordering detail worth noting: the reducer force-cancels every non-terminal tool call at turn end, so a subagent spawn's status must be read before the parent's terminal action is dispatched, or a live background spawn looks finished.

## Tests

Fourteen, including that a dropped completion closes the turn, a rejected call fails it, a pending call is left alone, a provider whose send returns early is untouched, a turn parked on a request the provider tracks or the user can see is untouched, a cancellation racing the close ends the turn once, a resolved subagent ends with its parent while a live background spawn does not, and a stale tool ready is denied.

Reverting the source and keeping the tests produces eight failures. Across the agent-host and Copilot suites: 1297 passing, 0 failing, with Copilot at 747 passing and unchanged. No new type errors, nothing under the synced protocol directory touched.

## Not included

No wall-clock or quiet-time trigger, and nothing keyed on the hang telemetry event. Those need tuning against real sessions and belong in a separate change.

Part of #333174.

title: build: make agent SDK tarballs a function of version and target
body:
Follow-up to #334094, which reverted a lockfile bump because the resulting tarball collided with an already-published CDN blob.

## The problem

CDN paths are content-addressed and immutable. `upload.ts` HEADs first and refuses to overwrite a blob whose sha256 differs. So the tarball at `agent-sdk/claude/<version>/<target>.tgz` has to be a function of the version and target and nothing else.

It wasn't. npm 7+ auto-installs `peerDependencies`, so 100 packages (`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`, `zod`, `ajv` and their graph) landed in `node_modules` and got tarred. Bump any of them transitively and the bytes change while the version does not, and the next upload fails against the published blob. That is what #333870 did.

## The fix

`npm ci --ignore-scripts --omit=peer`. A claude tarball is now exactly two packages, `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` and its `claude-agent-sdk-<target>` binary package, both pinned to the SDK version. Peer churn can no longer move the bytes.

The peers were never loaded from that tarball:

- `sdk.mjs` statically imports node builtins and nothing else. The one external module it resolves at runtime is its own native binary package. It inlines MCP, zod and ajv at publish time.
- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` is `import type` in all eight places it appears in non-test `src/`.
- `zod` is the interesting one. `claudeJsonSchemaToZod.ts` imports `z` at runtime, so this is *not* an unused dependency. But that zod is VS Code's own root dependency, shipped in the product, and the raw shapes it builds are passed *into* the SDK. Nothing resolves zod out of the downloaded tree. That narrower invariant is what `--omit=peer` actually needs, and it is what the load probe is built around.
- Empirically, an `--omit=peer` install drives a full MCP `initialize` / `tools/list` / `tools/call` round-trip with identical output.

Size is not the point. The peers are about 4% of a 90MB tarball.

`--omit=optional` would be a very different flag, since the native binary ships as an *optional* dependency. That is what `findMissingNativeOptionalDep` exists to catch.

Also bumps claude to **0.3.258** from 0.3.239, since the flag changes the bytes and the version has to move anyway. 0.3.258 adds `updateSettings` as a required `Query` member, so three test fakes get a stub. Worth flagging: the compile-time `_assertBindingsMatchSdk` drift check did *not* catch that, because it only covers bindings we opt into. The fakes' `implements Query` did the wider structural check by accident.

## Verifying it, for every SDK

That the SDK inlines its peers is an implementation detail Anthropic never promised, and the `peerDependencies` block says the opposite. So the assumption needs a guard. Since `--omit=peer` applies to *every* SDK, that guard cannot be special-cased to one. `Sdk` is an open string type, so adding an SDK is one folder under `agents/`, which would otherwise inherit the flag unchecked.

`verifyStagedTree` runs against the finished tree just before it is tarred, and every SDK must have a case. The `default` branch fails the build rather than skipping. The checks are deliberately different, because copying one onto the other would assert something we do not depend on.

**claude.** The agent host dynamic-imports `sdk.mjs` out of the tarball, so the build imports it too, in a child process and under a timeout. It then repeats the shipped call shape from `buildClientToolMcpServer`: a zod raw shape into `sdk.tool()`, the result into `createSdkMcpServer()`. Checking that the exports merely exist would miss a peer resolved lazily inside `tool()`. The native binary is then asserted present, non-empty and executable.

**codex.** The agent host never loads JS from that tarball. It spawns `vendor/<rust-triple>/bin/codex[.exe]` directly. So the check is structural: exactly one vendored triple, holding a runnable binary. `codexAgent.ts`'s `sdkTarget → triple` table is deliberately *not* copied here, because a second copy could drift and then validate a path nothing uses. A renamed triple stays the runtime's to catch.

Both are cross-target safe. The file checks are pure `stat`, and the claude probe only runs platform-independent JS that never reaches for the native binary.

## Drive-by

`chmodPlatformBinaries`'s claude branch looked for `claude` on every target, silently skipping win32's `claude.exe`. Nothing shipped broken, since the registry already publishes that binary `0755` and Windows ignores POSIX modes on extract. But the assumption was wrong, and the new assertion checks the same path the loop chmods. Both now derive the name from the target.

## Testing

Fault injection against a real extracted codex tree. Every check fires, and an untouched tree passes:

```
PASS  control: untouched tree passes
PASS  vendor/ missing
PASS  vendor/ has two triples
PASS  vendor/ has zero triples
PASS  binary missing
PASS  binary empty
PASS  binary not executable
PASS  unknown SDK ('gemini') hits the default branch
```

The claude probe is non-vacuous in three separate ways, each checked by substituting a broken SDK:

- a static peer import in `sdk.mjs` gives exit 1 with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`
- a `tool()` that resolves a peer from disk gives the same

title: Agent Host: surface remote connection state in sessions
body:
Remote agent host connection state was modelled well enough for the workspace picker, but nothing in the session surface consumed it. A session whose host had gone away sat in a permanent loading state with no explanation and no way out — several people resorted to bouncing through the workspace picker to force a reconnect.

This makes connection state a first-class part of the session surface.

## What a user sees

| State | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Cached session, host stopped | Perpetual spinner | Centered recovery state: **"Ubuntu is not running"** + primary **Start Ubuntu** button |
| Starting a host | Nothing | Live progress — `Downloading server (24%)`, `Waiting for agent host connection…` |
| Live session, host drops | Nothing | Inline banner, after a 1s quiet delay so brief blips stay silent |
| Reconnect backoff | `Reconnecting…` | **`Reconnecting to Ubuntu in 5s`**, counting down, with **Try Now** |
| Host unreachable (tunnel died) | `Cannot reach X`, dead end | Same message plus a **Retry** action |
| Host incompatible | Generic failure | Explicit "incompatible with this version" |

Opt-in **"Automatically Start WSL When Opening Chats"** (`chat.agentHost.wsl.autoStart`, default off) starts a stopped host instead of waiting for a click. Scoped per host *kind*, and per *outage* rather than per session — a mid-session drop gets its own attempt. Exposed through `IAgentHostAutoConnect` so any provider can back it however it likes; WSL is the only one wired up today.

**Try Now** accelerates the protocol client's in-place retry rather than redialling, so the outbox and session state survive.

## How it works

`ISession.remoteConnectionStatus` projects provider connection status into the session model (`undefined` for local sessions). `SessionRemoteConnection` owns presentation and recovery and derives exactly one surface — read-only banner, centered recovery, or connection banner — so the three can't fight over the same space. Disconnects carry a machine-readable reason (`HostNotRunning` vs `Unknown`) so the UI can tell "switched off, startable" from "unreachable".

The Start action is never rendered while an automatic start is pending: the content derivation itself returns the connecting presentation, so this holds structurally rather than depending on autorun ordering.

## Bugs found along the way

Three were pre-existing and reachable without any of this; the new UI just made them visible.

- A rejected connection factory (the path a stopped WSL distro actually takes) discarded the entry, so no status or reason ever reached consumers.
- The service fired its connection-change notification from *inside* a failing dial, before clearing the in-flight marker. Anything that dialled from that notification joined the dial that had just failed, so nothing reconnected and its `waitForConnection` never settled — an indefinite hang.
- WSL armed its idle timeout at spawn, so a cold VM boot legitimately producing no output for 60s was killed as idle. Split into separate startup (3 min) and idle (60s) budgets.

Each has a regression test that reproduces the original symptom — verified by reverting the fix and confirming the test hangs or times out rather than merely failing.

## Cleanup

Removed the `_clearConnectionOnRemoval` opt-out and its SSH/WebSocket overrides so clear-on-removal is uniform (a removed SSH host used to come back). Extracted the duplicated bootstrap-progress log parsing into a shared reporter. Replaced string disconnect reasons with a `const enum` including a required `Unknown`, so a new reason can't be silently forgotten. Dropped a redundant disconnect-reason map now that the status already carries it. Net ~190 lines of duplication and dead paths removed.

## Notes for reviewers

The duplication between `SessionRemoteConnectionStatus` and the platform status type is deliberate — it keeps `session.ts` free of platform imports. The exhaustive projection switch is what catches drift, and it did during this work.

Unifying this behind one status model is what makes the richer flows above possible at all; the previous per-transport implementations had no shared vocabulary to build on.

Tested by hand against WSL (stopped distro, mid-session shutdown, cold boot, reconnect) and tunnels.

title: agentHost: do not declare a connection dead while the host waits for our response
body:
The AHP liveness watchdog measured inbound silence only. When the agent host copies a client
customization bundle back over the connection, it sends reverse `resourceRead` requests and then
stays quiet while it waits for us. The client fills the client-to-host direction with large
responses, so the client `ping` queues behind that upload and cannot be answered. After 25s the
client closed a healthy tunnel.

Debug log bundles show this on 3 clients and 4 hosts: each host-side `Syncing plugin` is followed by
a client-side watchdog close and then a successful host-side `Reconnect`, so the host stayed
reachable. Whether the watchdog fired depended on unrelated inbound traffic that reset the read
timer. On one host the first sync took 43.7s and did not close, because an unrelated service
published actions every ~5.5s; the second sync ran while that service was quiet and closed at
exactly 25s.

A write-side timestamp is not a usable signal. RelayTransport gives bytes to a shared-process relay,
and the local tunnel process has its own buffer, so a recent write does not show what reached the
wire.

## agentHost: do not declare a connection dead while the host waits for our response

- Counts reverse requests that we received and did not answer, per transport. A count above zero
  shows that the peer waits for us.
- Defers the close while that count is above zero, and keeps the pre-existing high-load deferral in
  the same branch.
- Re-arms both timers at PING_INTERVAL_MS during a deferral, so the client continues to probe. Before
  this change one ping only was sent for each silent window.
- Grants a full PING_INTERVAL_MS + LIVENESS_TIMEOUT_MS window when the deferral clears. A response
  counts as answered when it goes to the transport, so the bytes that still drain and the host
  post-copy work need their own budget. Measured host-side gaps were 37-47s, thus the previous 5s
  re-arm still closed the connection.
- Keeps the grant to one for each deferral episode, so a dead transport is still detected.
- Does not change `_lastReadTime`, so the timeout diagnostic reports the true total silence.
- Injects a no-load estimator in the tests. The shared LoadEstimator singleton starts a 1s interval
  that does not drain under runWithFakedTimers, so these tests passed only when the suite around them
  disposed the client first.

## agentHost: keep a short revision history for each synced plugin

A client plugin nonce is a content hash, not a version that increases. A customization set that
changes and then returns to an earlier state makes a nonce that was synced before.
`_cleanupStaleNoncesFor` kept the current revision only, so each such cycle was a cache miss and
copied the full bundle again over the agent host connection.

- Keeps up to MAX_REVISIONS_PER_PLUGIN revisions for each plugin URI, so a customization set that
  returns to an earlier state is a cache hit.
- Changes the global cap from a plugin count to a revision count (DEFAULT_MAX_PLUGIN_REVISIONS). The
  LRU selects which revisions stay, so a plugin that syncs often keeps more history than an idle one.
- Removes cache entries whose directory does not exist when the cache loads. Such an entry cannot
  make a cache hit, and it uses one retention slot for the plugin and one slot in the global cap.
- Writes the nonce in the eviction logs. Before this change, a plugin that moved between revisions
  made identical log lines.

## Validation

- `scripts\test.bat --grep "watchdog"` — 10 passing
- `scripts\test.bat --grep "soft reconnect"` — 29 passing
- `scripts\test.bat --grep "AgentPluginManager"` — 16 passing
- `npm run typecheck-client` — clean
- Each new test also runs green on its own. `watchdog dead-transport detection triggers soft
  reconnect` failed in isolation before this change, on the clean baseline as well, for the same
  LoadEstimator reason; it now passes both in the suite and on its own.

## Notes for reviewers

- This reduces the false positives but does not remove them completely. If the drain and the host
  post-copy work take more than the full window after the last response goes to the transport, the
  watchdog can still fire. The window is now the documented 25s instead of 5s, and a new trace log
  reports the deferral duration and the outstanding request count.
- During a long deferral the client sends a ping every 5s, and each ping holds a `_pendingRequests`
  entry until a response arrives or the connection closes. This is about 9 entries for a 47s stall.

title: Revert claude agent SDK lockfile bump from #333870
body:
Reverts the `build/agent-sdk/agents/claude/package-lock.json` portion of #333870. The `dependencies-check.yml` and `build/npm/gyp/package-lock.json` changes from that PR stay.

## Why

The release build is red on every platform:

```
Error: [upload.ts] Blob already present with DIFFERENT sha256 metadata — refusing to overwrite content-addressed history.
  remote: 4d2a122a30085d088c124769fd01febd4814e1ce3022bf8534be3434103c58b6
  local:  3f428bf4db0ed63b7ff0587033a30e998eacaf246da933732764a0a8f8d6589f
```

#333870 bumped six transitive deps in the claude agent folder while `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` stayed pinned at `0.3.239`:

| package | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@hono/node-server` | 1.19.17 | 1.19.14 |
| `body-parser` | 2.3.0 | 2.2.2 |
| `body-parser/node_modules/content-type` | 2.1.0 | (removed) |
| `fast-uri` | 3.1.6 | 3.1.2 |
| `hono` | 4.13.4 | 4.12.25 |
| `ip-address` | 10.5.0 | 10.2.0 |

All six are `"peer": true`, so `npm ci` installs them into `node_modules`, and `node_modules` is exactly what `package.ts` tars. Different tree, different tarball, different sha.

The CDN path is `agent-sdk/claude/<version>/<target>.tgz`. Nothing in it reflects the transitive graph, so the SDK version can hold still while the content moves underneath it, and `upload.ts` correctly refuses to rewrite history. Codex passed in the same run because its lockfile wasn't touched.

This restores the lockfile to the state that produced the blobs already on the CDN. It was live on `main` from #333256 (Aug 28) until yesterday morning, so it is the known-good state, not a guess.

## Tradeoff, please read before approving

The revert reintroduces advisories that #333870 had cleared. `npm audit --package-lock-only` in `build/agent-sdk/agents/claude`:

- **main today:** 1 moderate (`qs`)
- **with this PR:** 6 findings, 1 low / 3 moderate / 2 high, adding `fast-uri`, `hono`, and `ip-address` on top of the same `qs` one

The high-severity pair is [GHSA-mwp4-54f8-5fhr](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mwp4-54f8-5fhr) and friends in `ip-address` (SSRF / trust-boundary bypass).

Worth weighing that these are peers pulled in behind the Claude SDK rather than code we call, but I did not chase down whether the SDK actually loads them, so treat the exposure as unquantified.

The alternative, if we would rather ship the newer deps than unblock cheaply: delete every blob under `agent-sdk/claude/0.3.239/` in the Azure Portal, not just `win32-arm64`, and re-run. Otherwise `0.3.239` means one dep graph on some platforms and another elsewhere. Note the blobs go up with `max-age=31536000, immutable`, so anyone who already cached the old tarball keeps it.

Happy to switch this PR to that approach instead if that is the call.

## This is the second time

#333636 made the identical lockfile edit on Aug 31 at 14:35 and was reverted 90 minutes later in `2b82959`, with a bare `This reverts commit ...` message and no explanation. Same failure, near-certainly. #333870 then re-landed the same bumps two days later.

## Follow-up

Not in this PR, but the invariant we actually depend on is "the whole lockfile is frozen unless the SDK version changes," and nothing enforces it. `build/agent-sdk/test/versionSync.test.ts` checks the SDK's own version in three places and says nothing about the other 109 entries. Options I can see:

1. Assert a hash of each `agents/*/package-lock.json` in that test, so touching transitive deps forces an explicit acknowledgement.
2. Put a lockfile hash in the blob path. Makes the content addressing honest, but breaks the one-URL-per-SDK-version assumption baked into `urlTemplate` and `product.agentSdks`.

I lean toward 1. Filing separately.

## Verification

- `cd build && node --test 'agent-sdk/**/*.test.ts'` passes.
- `package.json` is byte-identical between the two lockfile states, so `npm ci` stays in sync.
- Not verified locally: that the rebuilt tarball reproduces `4d2a122a…`. `chmodPlatformBinaries` sets `0o755`, which is a no-op on Windows, so a macOS-built tarball cannot match a pipeline-built one byte for byte. The release build is the real check.

title: Add a setting for the permission mode new Claude sessions start in
body:
Adds a setting for the permission mode new Claude sessions start in, so a user who always wants the same mode does not have to change it by hand every time.

## Today

`ClaudeAgent.resolveChatConfig` falls back to a hardcoded `permissionMode: 'default'` for any new session. The Agents window already replays a user's remembered last pick for sessions created there, but there is no setting, so the hardcoded value still governs every other creation path and every fresh profile.

## The setting

`chat.agentHost.claudeAgent.defaultPermissionMode`, defaulting to `default` so nothing changes for anyone who does not set it. Its enum and descriptions are Claude's existing five modes and their existing wording, not new text. It is read in exactly one place, the fallback in `resolveChatConfig`, and mirrored to a root config key through the repo's declarative mechanism rather than a hand-written forwarder.

A restored session keeps its own persisted mode: restore re-resolves through the same function with the persisted values, and `validateOrDefault` only consults the fallback when the incoming value is missing or invalid. A mode the user changes mid-session is untouched.

## Elevated modes are clamped by policy

`acceptEdits`, `auto` and `bypassPermissions` degrade to `default` while policy restricts auto-approval. Without this, a user in an organization that disables those modes could reinstate one through the setting. The same clamp already guards the equivalent new-session seed on the client side.

## Why Claude-scoped rather than one setting for every provider

The three providers do not share a vocabulary. Copilot uses `autoApprove` with `default`, `assisted` and `autoApprove`; Codex uses `codex.permissionsPreset` with `default`, `auto-review` and `full-access`. Only the token `default` is common. A single setting would need a mapping table asserting that, for instance, Claude's `acceptEdits` means the same as Copilot's `assisted`, which it does not, and a union enum would offer nine values of which six are silently ignored for any given provider.

Copilot needs no sibling: `chat.defaultConfiguration.approvals` already drives that axis for new sessions. Codex is genuinely uncovered and would be a reasonable follow-up.

## Why not a property on `chat.defaultConfiguration`

That object is client-side and speaks the platform vocabulary. This seam is host-side, in the provider that owns the mode, and applies to every client rather than only the ones that consult that object.

## Scope

`APPLICATION_MACHINE`, matching `chat.tools.global.autoApprove` and `chat.autoReply`. The practical effect is machine-scoped resolution, so a remote window reads and writes that machine's settings, which suits a mode a user may want inside a container but not locally. Like `chat.tools.global.autoApprove` it does not set `ignoreSync`.

## Tests

- `seeds a new chat from the configured default permission mode`
- `an elevated configured default degrades while policy restricts auto-approval`
- a regression guard that a restored session's persisted mode still outranks the setting

The first two fail without the change. `claudeAgent.test` 291 passing, 0 failing. No new type errors.

title: Keep observing a subagent whose chat outlives its spawning turn
body:
Keeps observing a subagent's chat when that chat outlives the turn that spawned it, so its tool calls are still claimed and executed and its turn can close.

Fixes #333931. #332073 shares this root.

## Defect

The client subscribes to a subagent's chat when it first sees the spawning tool call, but registers the release on the disposable store owned by the parent turn. When the parent turn ends, the subscription is torn down. If the subagent chat is created after that point, the in-flight subscribe is cancelled and the client never observes the chat again: nothing re-subscribes, since the server-initiated-turn watcher covers only the default chat and the enrichment path is restore-only.

The consequence is the reported hang. Client tool requests are read from session-level input-needed state, but execution is gated on a claimant that only the chat observer sets. With no observation there is no claim, so the tool is never executed and the subagent's turn never closes. A confirmation dispatched on that chat is likewise never rendered or answered.

Measured on a live host: the spawning tool call completed at 46.189 and the subagent chat was added at 48.316, two seconds after the parent turn had completed at 48.065. Across ten runs the subscribe failed exactly when the parent turn completed before the subagent chat was added, and never otherwise.

## Why the fix is here and not in the provider

Making the provider hold the parent turn open until the subagent starts looks smaller but is wrong. Background spawns are specified to outlive the parent turn: `drainForegroundSpawns` evicts only non-background entries and its documentation says background completions arrive later through a task notification, a background spawn's Task result deliberately does not fire `subagent_completed`, and turn completion is driven by the prompt queue, which never consults the subagent registry. A provider-side hold would wait forever on a background subagent, and on any foreground subagent that forwards no content. A parent-turn-scoped observation is therefore broken for background subagents independently of any race.

## Fix

Subagent observations are no longer owned by the parent turn's store. At turn end an observation whose child chat has not settled is moved into a session-scoped map instead of being disposed, and is released when the subagent settles, when a live in-turn observation supersedes it, or when the chat session tears down. Settled subagents are disposed exactly as before. The detached observer's progress sink is wrapped so it cannot emit into its parent's closed response, while the tool-call claim and tool-specific data, which do not go through the sink, keep working. A re-entrancy guard stops a nested subagent turn unwinding inside a detached observation from detaching back into the map being torn down.

## Tests

- `a subagent chat created after the parent turn completed is still observed`
- `a background subagent stays observed after the parent turn ends and is released when it finishes`
- `a subagent that finished during its parent turn is released when that turn ends`

The first two fail without the fix. `agentHostChatContribution.test` 369, `agentHostClientTools.test` 58, `stateToProgressAdapter.test` 149, and the whole agentSessions browser folder at 1338 passing, 0 failing. No new type errors.

The re-entrancy guard was not speculative: without it the client-tools suite failed its leak check on the nested second-level subagent test.

## Related, not addressed here

`_ensureAdditionalChatSubscription` keeps one non-refcounted reference per chat URI, so any single holder's release strands every other observer of that chat. The message router drops any message arriving while no turn is in flight, which can discard a background subagent's messages landing between turns. Both deserve their own changes.

Part of #333174.

title: Report a cancelled subscribe as cancelled, not as a missing resource
body:
Reports a subscribe that the client cancelled as a cancellation, instead of as a missing resource.

## Defect

`agentService.subscribe` throws `Subscription cancelled` when a subscription is released while it waits for a pending subagent chat to materialize. The protocol server's subscribe handler rewraps any non-protocol error as `Resource not found: <uri>`, and the request dispatcher logs it at error level. The result is an error line naming a resource that exists and was registered correctly. Four sibling sites threw the same plain error for the same concept, so the automation catalogue and reconnect paths reported it the same misleading way.

This is diagnostics only. It cost real investigation time: the message points at a host registration bug when the actual defect is on the client, which releases a subagent chat subscription when the parent turn ends.

## Fix

A `SubscriptionCancelledError extends ProtocolError`, thrown at all five sites with the message unchanged, so the discriminator is an `instanceof` rather than a string match. The subscribe handler logs it at info in the same style as the file's other benign lifecycle events, and `shouldLogFailedRequest` excludes it, which is what removes the error line.

`CancellationError` was the obvious candidate and is wrong here: its constructor forces the message to "Canceled", which would discard the resource URI, break two existing assertions and make the reconnect diagnostic less useful.

## Behaviour for a genuinely unknown resource is unchanged

`Cannot subscribe to unknown resource` stays a plain error, misses both new branches, and lands on the untouched final throw with the same code, message and error-level log. The test asserting that passed identically in the pre-fix and post-fix runs, which is the proof rather than an assertion of intent.

## Tests

- `cancelled subscribe reports cancellation, not a missing resource`
- `subscribe to an unknown resource still fails as a missing resource`

Without the fix the first reproduces the reported symptom exactly: an error-level `Resource not found` naming a resource that exists. `protocolServerHandler.test` 139 passing, `agentService.test` 405 passing, 0 failing. No new type errors.

## A cancelled subscribe whose resource never materialized

Added after tracing a second failure with the same symptom. The unknown-resource check ran before the cancellation check, so a subscribe that was both cancelled and whose resource never materialized reported "unknown resource" at error level. That is exactly the pending-subagent-chat case: when the wait times out because the client already released the subscription, the user got the misleading message this change exists to remove.

Testing cancellation first moves exactly one cell. With a live subscription and an undisposed store the cancellation guard is false and control reaches the identical unknown-resource throw, same message, same level, and the trailing catch keys on the same condition in both orders. Every pre-existing test expecting the unknown-resource message passes no `isActive` at all, so the guard is false and they cannot be reached by the swap.

Two tests: `a cancelled subscribe whose subagent chat never materializes reports cancellation, not an unknown resource`, and `a live subscription whose subagent chat never materializes still reports an unknown resource`, the second existing to pin the ordering so a future reorder cannot silently swallow real unknown-resource failures. The first fails without the change and reproduces the misleading message verbatim; the second passes in both orders, so it is not merely mirroring the change.

`agentService.test` 408 passing, `protocolServerHandler.test` 139, both with zero failures.

## Known limitation

No synced protocol error code describes cancellation, so the error keeps `AHP_SESSION_NOT_FOUND` and only the message and log level are corrected. A dedicated code would need a protocol change, noted in the class documentation.

Part of #333174.

title: Keep Codex MCP tool progress out of the tool result
body:
Keeps a Codex MCP tool's progress narration out of its result, routing it to the client's progress line instead, so the transcript and the model see the tool's real output and not the running commentary.

## Defect

`mapMcpToolCallProgress` appended each progress notification to `entry.output`, the same field real streamed output uses, and emitted the whole accumulation as tool content. Two consequences followed. When an MCP tool legitimately returned nothing, `mapItemCompleted` fell back to `entry.output`, so the concatenated narration became the persisted result content; an interrupted turn did the same for the orphaned completion. And each notification resent the ever-growing concatenation, one telemetry event each. The workbench renders that content as the tool's output embed and forwards it to MCP App webviews, so narration showed as output rather than progress. Claude does not merge progress and Copilot only trace-logs it; Codex was the outlier.

## Fix

Progress travels on `_meta` instead of in the content, since the protocol has no progress action and `_meta` is the sanctioned extension point. `mapMcpToolCallProgress` no longer touches `entry.output`; it coalesces repeats and emits `ChatToolCallContentChanged` carrying `_meta.progressMessage` (a new typed key on `IToolCallMeta`). The completion path uses only the real MCP output. The workbench reads `progressMessage` for a Running call and calls the tool invocation's `acceptProgress`, both on every Running update and when a client attaches mid-turn.

One related fix: `finalizeToolInvocation` now clears the progress before the tool is finalized. Without it, `didExecuteTool` promotes the last progress string to the past-tense label for any tool whose result carries no `toolResultMessage`, which the adapter never sets, so this affected every provider, not just Codex. A test pins it.

## Tests

Mapper: progress is not persisted as the result when the MCP result is empty, is not carried into an orphaned completion, is dropped after completion, coalesces identical messages, and does not clobber start-time meta. Meta reader: a progress message round-trips and a non-string one is dropped. Adapter: progress reaches the executing invocation, a missing or non-string value leaves it unchanged, and transient progress is not promoted to the past-tense message.

The empty-result test fails without the fix. Mapper 59, meta readers 32, adapter 152, all passing. No new type errors, nothing under the synced protocol directory touched.

Part of #333174.

title: Mark a turn interrupted by a host crash on restore
body:
Marks a turn that was in flight when the agent host died as interrupted on restore, so it renders as a clear error instead of silently closing as complete or cancelled.

## Why

Copilot detects a turn that was running when the host crashed, on restore, and marks it as an error, because its event log durably records abort, idle and error. Claude cannot: its transcript has no result or abort marker, so the replay mapper silently closes the trailing turn as complete (model was mid-text) or cancelled (a tool had no result), and the user is never told the host died mid-turn. This is provider-agnostic, so the fix is a chat contribution rather than a Claude-only change.

## What changed

A new `interruptedTurn` contribution keeps a durable open-turn marker in session metadata. On dispatch it writes `{ turnId, startedAt }` when a turn starts or resumes and clears it on any terminal action. On restore it reads the marker and, if the chat has no live turn, replaces the trailing turn with an `executionInterrupted` error part matching Copilot's wording and non-resumable status, matching the turn by id or, as a fallback, by start time. It never marks a turn that is already an error, never touches subagent chats, and never synthesizes a turn. It runs at order 150, after the turn-usage and delegation contributions attach their data to the same trailing turn.

Codex restores an in-progress rollout as complete, so the contribution applies to it too; a one second tolerance in the start-time fallback covers Codex widening whole-second timestamps. Copilot is a no-op through the already-error guard.

## Tests

Nine unit tests against a real contributions dispatcher and a test session database (marker written on start and cleared on every terminal action, the trailing turn marked on restore, already-error and subagent and predates-marker and live-turn cases left alone, the resume and floored-timestamp cases), plus `restore after an interrupted turn marks the trailing turn as an error` end to end through `getMessages`. Eight of nine fail without the contribution registered. `chatContributions.test` 69, `claudeAgent.test` 289, `agentService.test` 405, all passing. No new type errors, nothing under the synced protocol directory touched.

## Known window

If the host dies after a turn's terminal event but before the async marker clear lands, the restored turn is marked interrupted although it finished. This is the same class of window Copilot's own detection has.

title: Keep remote workspace folders when creating a session through the handler
body:
Keeps a remote window's workspace folders when a session is created through the handler path, so a dev container session is not created workspace-less.

## Defect

On first send, a session is created one of two ways. The provisional path, where the chat input picker pre-created the session, sends the raw workspace folders and works. The handler path, taken whenever no provisional session exists at send time (the picker never attached, or prewarm was silent because the folder was untrusted, or provisional creation failed), runs `_hostAddressableWorkingDirectories`, which keeps only folders whose unwrapped scheme equals the host's `defaultDirectory` scheme. The host reports that as `file:`, and a dev container window's folders are `vscode-remote://dev-container+...`, so every folder is dropped and the session is created with no working directories.

The consequences: the host marks a session with no working directories as workspace-less and runs the agent with no roots; the working-directory synchronizer refuses to touch a workspace-less session, so it never re-adds them; the session list's containment check finds nothing matching a workspace folder; and the same filtered set seeds the customization scope roots, so those are empty too.

## Fix

`_hostAddressableWorkingDirectories` keeps a folder when its unwrapped scheme is the host's scheme or `vscode-remote:`, mirroring `isSupportedWorkingDirectory` from #334005. Local `file:` folders take exactly the old branch, and the filter's original intent, dropping a scheme the host genuinely cannot address such as an `https:` virtual repository, is preserved.

Note that since #333296 the editor-remote transport rewrites same-authority `vscode-remote:` to `file:` on the wire, so the host stores `file:` on that path; keeping `vscode-remote:` here is still correct and consistent with the host-side predicate on every path.

## Tests

- a remote window with two `vscode-remote:` folders creates the session with both
- a local window with `file:` folders is unchanged
- an `https:` folder next to a remote one is still dropped while the remote one is kept

The two remote tests fail without the fix. The browser-layer file runs under the Electron test runner: whole file 369 passing, 0 failing. No new type errors.

title: Expose the Claude replay attribution index
body:
Exposes the tool-call attribution index the Claude replay mapper already builds, instead of discarding it, and adds a pure resolver that derives what a restored session should know from it. Foundation only: nothing hydrates a live session yet.

## Why

On restore, `mapSessionMessagesToTurns` builds an index of every `tool_use` (its announcing turn, name, client-tool flag, input) in order to attach results, then returns only the turns. Everything that would let a late `tool_result` or a subagent completion be attributed after a restart is thrown away, so those envelopes fall into the unknown-id path and are dropped. That is the durable-state half of the replay and attribution findings under #333174; the live-session half (hydrating on resume, consulting the index in the mapper, draining on rebind) follows in a separate change so that it can land after #334008.

## What changed

- `replaySessionMessages` returns `{ turns, attribution }`, where the attribution carries one entry per `tool_use` (`toolUseId`, `turnId`, `toolName`, `isClientTool`, `parsedInput`, `isSubagentSpawn`, `resultSeen`, `agentId` when a Task result carried the suffix) plus `tailTurnId`. `mapSessionMessagesToTurns` is a wrapper returning the turns, so callers are unchanged. Same single pass, no I/O.
- New pure `claudeAttributionResolver`: `buildAttributionSeed` retains every unresolved entry as pending, and `hydrateAttribution` seeds the tool-call registry through a new `hydrate` that shares the live insertion and info-writing paths, so display strings stay identical.

An earlier revision classified an unresolved call in a non-tail turn as dead, on the reasoning that a later user envelope proves its result can never arrive. That is wrong during a steering preempt: the steer is persisted as a later user envelope while a tool from the preempted request can still return, which is the case #334008 addresses. Replay data cannot reliably distinguish a steer folded into the running request from a genuine later turn, since the synthetic and meta markers are not carried through, so the seed now conservatively retains everything that might still receive a result. The `dead` bucket remains in the shape, documented as reserved for a future steer-aware transcript, and is currently always empty.

## Tests

- `replaySessionMessages exposes the attribution index alongside the turns` (also asserts the wrapper's output is deep-equal to the same pass)
- `buildAttributionSeed: an unresolved tool_use in a non-tail turn is retained as pending, not dead, because a later steer may still return its result`
- `hydrateAttribution seeds registry info so pastTenseMessage parity holds, hydrates non-tail pending entries, and records spawns`

Replay mapper 30, resolver 3, subagent registry 9, `claudeAgent.test` 288, all passing. No new type errors, eslint clean.

title: Fail Claude client tool calls that no connected client provides
body:
Fails a Claude client tool call that no connected client provides, visibly and immediately, instead of leaving it parked forever.

## Defect

A client tool is executed by whichever window contributed it. When no connected window provides the tool, the stream mapper stamps no contributor on the call, so the session-input contribution never publishes an execution request, the protocol server's disconnect grace timeout never arms (it is gated on a contributor), and the in-process MCP handler parks on the pending-request registry with nothing that will ever answer. The protocol server's own comment says ownerless calls "are failed immediately by the provider". That is true for Copilot, which fails the call and delivers the failure into its registry, and was false for Claude: nothing in the Claude harness did it.

There is a second half. In `default` permission mode the SDK still asks `canUseTool` for the tool, and the host drops a permission ask for a call that is already terminal without answering it, so even a failed call would leave the SDK parked in `canUseTool`.

## Fix

- The mapper remembers at `content_block_start` that a client tool has no owner and, at `content_block_stop`, appends `ChatToolCallComplete` with `{ success: false, error: { code: 'toolUnavailable', message } }` right after the `ChatToolCallReady` it already emits, using the workbench's error shape and code and Copilot's wording. It has to follow Ready, since the reducer ignores a completion while the call is still streaming. The subagent path emits the same failure for an inner tool and tags it with the parent.
- The session recognises that completion by its error code at the point where it already inspects mapper signals, pre-answers the permission request so the SDK reaches the handler, and delivers the failure into the client-tool registry with `respondOrBuffer`, so the handler's later `register` resolves at once with an `isError` result.

The SDK's own later `tool_result` still drains to a second completion that the reducer and the tool-call tracker both drop, which keeps the drain path warning-free; a test pins that. `mapResult` is untouched, and nothing overlaps #334037 or #334038.

## Tests

- `an mcp__client__* tool with no owner gets no contributor and is failed at content_block_stop`
- `inner client tools with no owner are failed immediately, tagged with the parent`
- `a client tool with no active client owner is failed immediately and its parked handler resolves with an error`, plus the subagent variant, driving the real MCP handler and `requestPermission`

All fail without the fix: the handler and the permission both report parked. `claudeAgent.test` 290, mapper 33, subagent signals 13, all passing. No new type errors, eslint clean.

## Left for a separate change

`_handleToolReady` returning on a stale ready without answering the permission request leaks the SDK's `canUseTool` for any tool that reaches a terminal state before its ask arrives. This change works around it for the ownerless case only; the general fix belongs with the abandoned-turn work.

title: Retire a stranded optimistic chat truncation once the host has applied it
body:
Retires a stranded optimistic `chat/truncated` once the host has evidently applied it, so it stops being replayed over every later turn and blanking the transcript.

## Defect

The client applies its own dispatched chat actions optimistically, keeps them pending, and `_recomputeOptimistic` replays every still-pending action over confirmed state on each confirmed envelope. Retirement was echo-only, keyed on `origin.clientSeq`, with one non-echo exception for a pending turn start. `chat/truncated` is client-dispatchable and destructive: it clears `activeTurn` and, with no `turnId`, the whole turn list. The workbench dispatches it right before `chat/turnStarted` when starting a turn. If the host applies it without echoing the client sequence, the pending truncation is replayed on every later envelope and empties the transcript for as long as it stays pending. The reducer cannot help: `reduce(reduce(s, a), a)` already equals `reduce(s, a)`; the harm is a destructive action replayed over a state that has legitimately moved on, which a pure reducer cannot detect. #334011 makes the turn-start case safe in the reducer; this is the overlay-side fix for truncation.

## Fix

`ChatStateSubscription` retires a pending truncation on either of two observations: a confirmed truncation for the same `turnId` arrives without a matching origin, or the client's own later `chat/turnStarted` is confirmed, since dispatch is ordered and the truncation must have been applied first. Retirement folds the action into confirmed state rather than dropping it, so the pre-truncation turns are not resurrected. The find-splice-apply loop the turn-start promotion had inline is extracted as `_retirePending`, so the next non-echoing destructive action adds one predicate rather than another loop. `_reconcile` now drops the echoed entry before any promotion, which is required for correctness: promoting an earlier pending entry before the old splice would have shifted the index and removed the wrong entry. Echo semantics are unchanged.

## Tests

- `a stranded optimistic truncation is retired when the host confirms the same truncation without an origin`
- `a stranded optimistic truncation is retired once a later client-dispatched turn start is confirmed`
- `an optimistic truncation that has not been observed is still replayed` (negative control)
- `an optimistic truncation dispatched after the confirmed turn start stays pending` (ordering guard)

The first two fail without the fix. `agentSubscription.test`: 64 passing, 0 failing. No new type errors, nothing under the synced protocol directory touched.

Part of #333174.

title: Answer client-tool handler rejections as tool errors
body:
Makes the Claude client-tool MCP handler answer a rejected wait as a tool error instead of throwing, and makes a duplicate registration of a parked request share the existing wait instead of cancelling it.

## Defects

The in-process MCP handler for client tools awaits `registry.register(toolUseId)` with no try/catch, so a rejection propagates out of the handler into the SDK's tool path. Rejections happen: `rejectAll` on rebind and dispose rejects every parked request, and until now `register` on a key that was already parked rejected the previous waiter with a cancellation. The MCP SDK converts a thrown handler error into a bare tool error, so the model received "Canceled" with no context, and the host's own shape for a failed tool was bypassed. Copilot's handler guards this explicitly; Claude's did not.

## Fix

- The handler catches a rejected wait and returns `{ isError: true }` with a text block naming the tool and the reason, the same shape the sibling server-tool handler and the handler's own missing-id branch already use. The handler never throws.
- `register` on a key that is already parked returns the existing promise, so every waiter settles on the single response.

Every caller of `register` was checked. Copilot's client-tool path catches, logs and rethrows, so a duplicate no longer cancels its first invocation. Copilot's permission and unsandboxed-command confirmations use the same key sequentially and would now share one answer if they ever overlapped, rather than throwing out of the permission handler. Codex's client-tool path stops producing a spurious "was cancelled" failure on a replay. The `rejectAll` and `denyAll` sweeps are unchanged, so abort and dispose behave as before.

## Tests

- `a duplicate register for a parked key shares the deferred`
- `handler maps a rejected awaitResult to an isError result instead of throwing`

Both fail without their fix, with "Canceled" surfacing from the registry and the handler respectively. Registry 15 passing, handler 11 passing, `claudeAgent.test` 288, `copilotAgentSession.test` 413, `copilotAgent.test` 335, `codexCreateChat.test` 57, all 0 failing. No new type errors.
