title: sessions: track manually typed characters in session summary telemetry
body:
Adds two fields to the `agents/sessionSummary` telemetry event that report how much the user hand-edited a session's workspace rather than letting the agent do the work:

- **`typedCharacters`** — characters the user manually typed into files inside the session's workspace folders.
- **`typedFileCount`** — how many distinct such files they typed into.

## How it works

A new `SessionsTypedCharactersTracker` observes the text models of the window it runs in and counts only edits that pass the editor's existing `isUserEdit()` predicate, so agent edits, accepted suggestions, paste and undo/redo are all excluded.

The Agents window is a separate renderer with its own `IModelService`, so the "don't capture typing done in a regular window" requirement falls out of the architecture: models from another window never reach this tracker.

Typing fires one content change per keystroke, so counts are buffered per resource and flushed in batches rather than persisting on every key.

## Notes for reviewers

Three decisions worth a look:

- **Attribution is to the active session only.** An earlier revision scanned every known session per flush; that was wasteful, and the user only edits the session they are looking at. Because flushing is batched, the active session is cached and the buffer flushed *before* adopting a new one — otherwise typing in session A followed by a quick switch to B would land on B.
- **Resources are matched against `folder.workingDirectory`, not `folder.root`.** For a worktree session the root is the shared repository checkout, which the session itself never edits, so matching the root would misattribute. The folder check also keeps typing in the chat input box (itself a text model) out of the count.
- **File identity is persisted as a hash, capped at 250 per session.** The lifecycle tracker persists to application storage, so keeping raw URIs would put the user's file paths on disk for the lifetime of every tracked session. Only the count is ever reported.

## Drive-by fix

`folderCount` / `gitFolderCount` / `nonGitFolderCount` / `isMultiRoot` were captured once when a session was first observed and never refreshed, so a session whose workspace resolved asynchronously or gained folders later reported stale counts. They are now refreshed on each interaction (skipping empty/unresolved workspaces, so teardown does not overwrite good values with zeros). Classification comments updated to match.

## Validation

`typecheck-client`, `eslint` and `valid-layers-check` are clean; **180 tests pass** across the full sessions contrib suite. New tests cover the user-edit predicate, per-resource batching, model add/remove, distinct-file counting with cap saturation, working-directory scoping, attribution across a session switch, and last-observed folder counts.

`npm run hygiene` fails in this environment at its first step with a doubled drive letter (`C:\C:\...\remote\package.json`) — reproduced identically on a clean tree, so it is pre-existing and unrelated.

title: git: don't reveal deleted resources in OS file explorer
body:
Fixes #332749

## Summary

`git.revealFileInOS` (Reveal in File Explorer / Finder / Open Containing Folder) and `git.revealInExplorer` are contributed to the `scm/resourceState/context` menu for every Source Control resource, including resources with `Status.DELETED` / `INDEX_DELETED` / `BOTH_DELETED`.

The menu's `when` clause can only check `scmResourceGroup` / `remoteName` / platform — there's no per-resource-status context key available to hide these entries only for deleted files, so they stay visible and clickable even though the target path no longer exists on disk.

Clicking them currently does nothing observable: the underlying `shell.showItemInFolder` (and the Explorer/Finder reveal command) is a no-op when the path is missing, so the user gets no feedback at all.

## Fix

Guard both commands the same way `git.openFile` already guards against deleted resources (see its existing `.filter(r => r.type !== Status.DELETED && r.type !== Status.INDEX_DELETED)`), and show a warning message instead of failing silently.

`DELETED_BY_US` / `DELETED_BY_THEM` (modify/delete merge conflicts) are intentionally left unaffected — verified that git leaves the "theirs"/"ours" content in the working tree for those, so there is something real to reveal.

## Test plan

- [x] Deleted file (working tree) → warning shown, no reveal attempted
- [x] Modified/existing file → reveals normally, unaffected
- [x] Modify/delete merge conflict (`DELETED_BY_US`) → reveals normally, unaffected
- [x] `tsc --noEmit` passes

title: Local history: await model resolution before merge window decision
body:
<!-- Thank you for submitting a Pull Request. Please:

Fixes #332737

`WorkingCopyHistoryModel.addEntry` decided whether to replace the latest entry (merge window) by reading `this.entries.at(-1)` without awaiting model resolution first, unlike every other entry-mutating path (`removeEntry`, `updateEntry`, `getEntries`, `store`). On a freshly constructed model - first save of a file after window start or reload - `entries` is still empty even when `entries.json` on disk holds a same-source entry seconds old, so the merge-window replacement is skipped and a duplicate history entry is created.

The fix awaits resolution at the top of `addEntry`, mirroring `doStore`. Resolution is memoized and only reads from disk, so there is no deadlock and no reordering for already-resolved models; the observable change is confined to fresh models, where add/replace events now fire after the disk read they depend on anyway.

Draft until #332737 receives triage.

## How was this tested

```
node build/next/index.ts transpile
".build/electron/Code - OSS.exe" test/unit/electron/index.js --crash-reporter-directory=.build/crashes --run vs/workbench/services/workingCopy/test/electron-browser/workingCopyHistoryService.test.js
```

A new test reproduces the reload cycle end to end over a shared in-memory file system: save an entry, dispose the service, recreate it (fresh unresolved model), save again within the merge window, and assert one merged entry results. Against the unfixed source it fails with two entries (`2 !== 1`); with this change the suite runs 21 passing, 0 failing, and the adjacent working copy suites pass unchanged (tracker 27, backup service 58, backup tracker 77).

title: Streams: settle pending writes when a writeable stream is destroyed
body:
<!-- Thank you for submitting a Pull Request. Please:
* Read our Pull Request guidelines:
  https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/wiki/How-to-Contribute#pull-requests
* Associate an issue with the Pull Request.
* Ensure that the code is up-to-date with the `main` branch.
* Include a description of the proposed changes and how to test them.

Fixes #332730

`WriteableStream.destroy()` cleared `pendingWritePromises` without settling it, so every producer parked inside `await stream.write()` under backpressure stayed parked forever after a destroy. Reachable through the file service copy pipeline: when a consumer stream created with a `highWaterMark` is destroyed mid-transfer, the read loop in `io.ts` never returns from its awaited write and the `finally` that closes the source file handle never runs. The codebase already treats this hang class as a bug elsewhere (`ResourceQueue.dispose` releases its drainers "to prevent hanging promises").

The fix stores pending writes as resolve/reject pairs and has `destroy()` reject them all with an error, mirroring how dispose paths elsewhere release waiters. Writing to an already-destroyed stream kept its existing silent no-op; only the parked-writer hang is addressed.

Draft until #332730 receives triage.

## How was this tested

```
node build/next/index.ts transpile
node node_modules/mocha/bin/mocha.js test/unit/node/index.js --delay --ui=tdd --timeout=5000 --exit --run out/vs/base/test/common/stream.test.js
```

Two tests were added next to the highWaterMark block: destroying a stream with a pending backpressure write now settles that write (the pre-fix run fails this test by timing out on the literal hang), and writing to a destroyed stream keeps returning synchronously instead of queueing. Before the production change: 26 passing, 1 failing; after: 27 passing, 0 failing.

Additional verification performed during development:

- every production caller that creates streams with a highWaterMark was audited (`htmlFileSystemProvider`, `fileImportExport`, `agentHostRequestService`): all wrap their awaited write in try/catch, so the new rejection is handled and previously hung paths now unwind to their cleanup
- streams without a highWaterMark never produce pending write promises, so their destroy behavior is unchanged

title: refactor handling of enabled/disabled state of built-in skills in the Agents window
body:
## Summary

This restores Enable/Disable support for built-in skills in the Agent Host Customizations UI while keeping `PureItemProviderItemSource` a pure projection of provider output.

Enabled built-in skills are synchronized to the Agent Host as user customizations. The Agent Host merges them with the customizations it discovers and publishes the resulting set back to VS Code through its item provider.

Disabled built-in skills require special handling because they are intentionally excluded before synchronization and therefore cannot be returned by the Agent Host. To keep them visible and allow users to re-enable them, the Agent Host item provider supplements its output with locally known disabled built-in skills.

The implementation:

- Restricts user enablement state to built-in skills. Other customization types and storage sources are unaffected.
- Marks user-disabled built-in skills during local customization enumeration.
- Excludes disabled built-in skills before creating the customization bundle sent to the Agent Host.
- Adds missing disabled built-in skills to the item provider output with `enabled: false`, preserving their original URI so the existing Enable action can update the correct prompts-service entry.
- Overrides stale enabled provider rows while synchronization is in progress, avoiding duplicate or temporarily enabled entries.
- Forwards skill enablement changes through the item provider’s `onDidChange` event.
- Keeps `PureItemProviderItemSource` unchanged: it continues to listen only to the provider and render provider output.
- Reuses the existing Customizations UI actions and context-key conditions, which expose Enable/Disable only for built-in skills.

The resulting refresh flow is:

```text
Enable/Disable action
→ update prompts-service disabled set
→ skill-change event
→ item-provider change event
→ item-source cache invalidation
→ items-model refetch
→ Customizations UI update
```

title: Ternary search tree: make has agree with get
body:

Fixes #332721

`TernarySearchTree.has` reported true for any strict prefix of a stored key, because its condition accepted nodes that merely have a `mid` chain:

```ts
return !(node?.value === undefined && node?.mid === undefined);
```

so after `set('foobar', 1)` a lookup of `foo`, `fo` or `f` returned true while `get` returned undefined for the same keys. The separate `hasElementOrSubtree` method exists precisely for subtree-existence semantics; exact-key membership is what `has` was meant to provide. The fix makes `has(key)` agree with `get(key) !== undefined`.

Reachable effects of the loose form: the context key service takes a `has` shortcut before falling back to settings, so asking for `config.editor` after only `config.editor.fontSize` was cached yielded undefined instead of the composed value; and the parcel file watcher treated a request path that is a prefix of an already-watched path as already watched, adding a redundant recursive watcher.

Draft until #332721 receives triage.

## How was this tested

```
node build/next/index.ts transpile
node test/unit/node/index.js --run out/vs/base/test/common/ternarySearchtree.test.js
```

A new test pins prefix lookups (`has('foobar')` true, `has('foo')`/`has('f')`/`has('x')` false, `get('foo')` undefined) plus a falsy-value case (`set('bar', 0)`, `has('bar')` true). Against the unfixed source the prefix assertions fail; with this change: 33 passing, 0 failing.

Additional verification performed during development:

- randomized shared-prefix trials with delete/deleteSuperstr interleaved: new implementation agrees with `get() !== undefined` on every probe (~24k), while the old one diverged on ~42% of probes
- all four production call sites audited (`contextKeyService` change listener and getValue shortcut, parcel watcher dedupe, explorer ignore tree): none depends on the prefix-true behavior, three strictly benefit

body:

Fixes #332715

`TernarySearchTree.deleteSuperstr` cleared all three child links of the prefix node, but only the `mid` chain holds superstrings; `left` and `right` hold unrelated keys that merely sort around that character position. Deleting a prefix therefore wiped unrelated entries: with config-shaped keys, deleting superstrings of `config.editor` emptied a trie that also held `config.files.autoSave`. The context key service calls this on every non-default-source settings change, so unrelated cached context values vanished and stayed missing from `collectAllValues()` until something recomputed them.

Three coordinated corrections in `_delete`, all serving that one semantics:

- the superstring branch clears only `node.mid`;
- with left/right surviving, the value-less prefix node can now reach the BST removal path whose successor copy previously orphaned the successor's own equal-child chain; that chain moves up together with the copied segment (this also fixes the same loss in plain `delete()`, reproducible today with keys `ab, aa, ac, acd`);
- the removal guard no longer treats stored falsy values as absent, so an exact key holding `0`, `false` or `''` survives deleting its superstrings.

Draft until #332715 receives triage.

## How was this tested

```
node build/next/index.ts transpile
node test/unit/node/index.js --run out/vs/base/test/common/ternarySearchtree.test.js
```

Two new tests pin sibling survival for strings and for config-key segments (including the both-side-sibling shape that reaches the successor-copy path), one pins falsy exact-key retention, and one existing expectation in the config delete_superstr test was corrected: it previously required `config.boo` to vanish even though that key does not extend the deleted prefix - it could only pass because of the bug. Before the change the suite measures 33 passing with 2 failing new assertions; after it, 35 passing, 0 failing.

Additional verification performed during development:

- randomized old-vs-new differential across all four iterator factories (strings, paths, config keys, uris) against a reference model enforcing "remove keys strictly extending the prefix, keep the exact key": zero divergences for the new code over ~120k operations, balance asserted after every operation

title: perf: keep session lookups out of per-file agent feedback loops
body:
Narrow fix for the feedback/annotations part of #332670.

Switching sessions could block the renderer for seconds. The agent feedback overlay iterates every original/modified URI of the active multi-diff and did **session-scoped** work per file: `getFeedbackSessionResource()` -> `getFeedback()` -> `getSessionEditorComments()`. Every one of those ends up calling `ISessionsManagementService.getSession()`, which rebuilds each provider's session catalog and then scans it linearly. With a 6,600-file Changes editor that is ~13k catalog rebuilds; a session with *no* feedback is the worst case because nothing stops the scan early.

### Changes

- `AgentFeedbackService._resolveSession()`: resolve through the active `IActiveSession` facade when the requested resource is the active session, and otherwise from a single-entry memo of the last lookup (hit **or** miss). The memo is dropped on `onDidChangeSessions` and when the session is deleted, so it never outlives a catalog change. Used by `getSessionForFile()`, `_isAgentHostSession()` and `_sessionContainsResource()` - the last two run on every `getFeedback()` call.
- `getFeedbackSessionCandidates()`: lazily maps resource candidates to their feedback session and yields each distinct session at most once, so feedback/backend work runs once per session instead of once per file. Used by the editor overlay and the feedback editor actions; both keep their early exit once a session with comments is found.
- `getSessionForFile()` now checks file eligibility before resolving anything (same result, no lookup for ineligible resources).

### Tests

New unit tests cover the dedupe over a 4,000-candidate multi-diff (including that iteration stops resolving once the caller breaks) and the session resolution: active session needs no management-service lookup, a non-active session is looked up once until sessions change, and an unknown session is remembered as unknown.

Not addressed here (separate areas from the issue): the archived worktree lifecycle and the `getSession()` lookup contract itself.

title: Fix New Chat Window crash by creating the parked chat pet host in the main window realm
body:
## Description

Opening **New Chat Window** failed immediately with `Not allowed to create elements in child window JavaScript context.`, leaving the chat editor unrendered.

`ChatPetWidgetCoordinator.createDormantHost` created the parked pet host through the *host's* owner document. In an auxiliary window that document's `createElement` is replaced with a throwing stub by `BrowserAuxiliaryWindowService.createContainer`, so the first pet-host registration in that window threw during `ChatWidget.render` → `EditorPane.createEditor`.

Regressed in 1cecb47 (#332153), which introduced the coordinator.

### Changes

- `createDormantHost()` builds its detached parent with `dom.$` — the main window realm, matching how `ChatPetWidget` creates the rest of its DOM. The host argument was only used for its owner document and is dropped.

```diff
-	private createDormantHost(host: IChatPetWidgetHost): IChatPetWidgetHost {
-		const parent = host.parent.ownerDocument.createElement('div');
+	private createDormantHost(): IChatPetWidgetHost {
+		// Auxiliary windows forbid `createElement` on their own document, so the
+		// parked host is created in the main window realm.
+		const parent = dom.$('div');
```

- Regression test registering a pet host owned by an auxiliary document whose `createElement` throws (the established iframe pattern used by `voiceGlow`/`chatClipboard` tests); it reproduces the reported stack without the fix. `createHost()` in the suite now accepts an optional parent.

The parked element is never attached, so only its owner document changes; host activation still re-parents the overlay into the real (auxiliary) host.

### Not addressed

`chatRichLink.ts` and `sessions/.../chatBackgroundRenderer.ts` have the same `ownerDocument.createElement` pattern and are separate latent issues; left out to keep this fix scoped.

title: agent host: start persistent Codex app-server only for Codex sessions
body:
## Problem

Fixes https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-internalbacklog/issues/8883

Opening VS Code with existing ChatGPT credentials started and retained a Codex app-server even when Codex was never selected. Startup account, model, and session metadata reads went through the same lazy boundary and could accidentally promote that process to a persistent runtime.

## Behavior after this change

- Startup uses a bounded one-off app-server probe to populate the signed-in ChatGPT account card with email, plan, profile image, and rate limits, then shuts it down.
- Passive model and session catalogue reads do not retain a Codex process.
- Creating a Codex session or restoring an existing one is the explicit activation point that starts and retains the app-server.
- Activation schedules a fresh model refresh so ChatGPT subscription models remain available after an Agent Host restart.
- The account card is populated consistently before and after persistent activation.

## Why the provider and session-registry changes are needed

Once passive session listing no longer activates Codex, it cannot always ask the provider for authoritative thread metadata. Returning no metadata would make registered Codex sessions disappear. Falling back only to their creation time would corrupt recency sorting and external-session filtering after an Agent Host restart.

This change therefore:

- adds optional in-process metadata-read options that distinguish passive catalogue reads from explicit session restore;
- lets Codex accept host-owned `startTime` and `modifiedTime` fallbacks while it is inactive;
- persists `modifiedTime` in the local Agent Host registry and only advances it monotonically; and
- activates Codex for authoritative metadata only when a session is restored.

This does **not** change the Agent Host wire protocol, message shapes, methods, or versioning. `modifiedTime` already exists in session metadata; the registry changes preserve its correct value while the provider is inactive.

## Additional lifecycle hardening

- replace stale app-server connections without disposing the newly installed connection;
- roll back failed chat creation and clean up orphaned provider threads; and
- serialize customization and model refresh work so activation reliably publishes subscription models.

## Verification

- `npm run compile-client`: 0 errors
- `npm run hygiene`: 11,500 files clean
- Codex model-refresh suite: 49 passing
- `git diff --check`: clean
- dap-cli attached to the isolated Agent Host, confirmed the expected process, and resumed it cleanly
- after `Developer: Restart Local Agent Host`, dap-cli stopped in Codex activation with an ambient refresh already in flight; the serialized follow-up refresh then published the ChatGPT subscription catalogue
- the isolated Code OSS model picker showed `GPT-5.6-Sol` under the `ChatGPT` section after two Agent Host restarts
- isolated Code OSS logs confirmed the startup probe starts, reads the signed-in ChatGPT account, and stops without persistent activation
- with Copilot selected, process inspection confirmed no Codex child remained; selecting Codex then created the persistent app-server child
- the Agents account card showed the signed-in email, ChatGPT Plus plan, profile image, and rate limit before activation, and its rendered content was identical after persistent activation

title: Split session artifacts into artifacts and references
body:
An artifact is something the session produced that is not an ordinary workspace edit: a pull request or issue it opened, a plan file written outside the workspace, another side effect of its work. A reference is something it did not produce but the user should look at because of the task: the pull request or commit that introduced a bug, a relevant page.

The agent now says which it recorded through a mandatory `isArtifact` flag, so the tools are renamed to `add_artifact_or_reference`, `remove_artifact_or_reference` and `list_artifacts_and_references`, and the per-type `createdByThisSession` field is gone — being produced by the session is the definition of an artifact. Entries persisted before this change read back as artifacts. Tool calls render "Added artifact" or "Added reference" from the flag; removal takes its wording from what it actually removed.

References get their own pill, always summarized as a count, placed directly after the artifacts pill so the two read as a pair. Only artifacts are promoted into the pull request and issue pills, which poll GitHub, but a reference keeps its link identity so anything those pills already show is offered exactly once.

### Along the way

- The artifacts pill no longer collapses into a lone entry unless it is a file, whose name and themed icon say what it is; every other single artifact stays behind "1 Artifact" so the row keeps a stable shape. `alwaysSummarize` becomes a `ChatPillSingleEntry` policy interpreted in one place.
- Parsing GitHub issue and pull request references out of user messages is removed. It fed the same pills from a second source, which would show a recorded reference twice, and it guessed at intent the agent can now state outright.
- A `uri` the client cannot open is rejected when it is recorded, instead of being reported as added and then appearing in no pill at all.
- Reading persisted artifacts reports what it could not parse, so a corrupt row no longer empties a session's artifacts without a trace.

### Notes

- The new `SessionChatPills_ReferenceSingle` and `SessionChatPills_ArtifactsAndReferences` fixtures need a screenshot baseline from CI.
- One consequence of the compatibility rule, called out deliberately: a pull request persisted before this change with `createdByThisSession: false` reads back as an artifact and can therefore become the session's main pull request. It only affects sessions that recorded someone else's pull request.

### Validation

`tsc --noEmit`, eslint over every changed file, `valid-layers-check`, and the affected node and chromium suites all pass.

title: Resolve session-relative changeset URI templates from remote agent hosts
body:
The changes view reads a session's changeset catalogue and subscribes to each entry's `uriTemplate`. It parsed that template verbatim, which is only correct when the host publishes a fully-qualified URI.

VS Code's own agent host publishes exactly that — `buildDefaultChangesetCatalog` bakes the session URI into every entry:

```ts
uriTemplate: buildBranchChangesetUri(sessionUri),   // → ahp-session:/abc/changeset/branch
```

So the client never had to resolve anything, and local sessions worked. Host and client shared an assumption that held as long as both were VS Code.

A remote agent host publishes the catalogue relative to the session channel instead:

```
changeset/session   changeset/branch   changeset/uncommitted
changeset/all       changeset/turn/{turnId}
```

`URI.parse('changeset/branch')` yields `file:///changeset/branch` — a path on the client's own filesystem. From a live remote session:

```
SUB id=21  file:///changeset/branch   ← -32008 not found
SUB id=41  file:///changeset/session  ← -32008 not found
```

Every static changeset resolved to something the host had never heard of, so the changes view stayed on "No Changed Files" with nothing logged.

## Why only the changes view

The chat response summary builds its turn-changeset URI from the session itself via `buildTurnChangesetUri(...)` and ignores the catalogue, so it kept reporting the same edits correctly. Two consumers, same session, same host — one worked. That asymmetry is what isolated the bug.

## The fix

`resolveChangesetUriTemplate(sessionUri, uriTemplate)` joins a session-relative template onto the session channel and returns a fully-qualified one unchanged, tested by an RFC 3986 scheme prefix.

The resolved URI is byte-identical to what `buildBranchChangesetUri` and friends already produce, so this converges on the shape the rest of the codebase builds rather than inventing one.

It lives in `changesetUri.ts` beside the other changeset URI helpers, and is applied once in `createChangesets` where the session URI is already in scope — so the static changesets and the per-turn one are all covered without touching either changeset class.

The template is still read from the catalogue at runtime; it is resolved before use, not reconstructed.

## Risk

A fully-qualified template takes an early return and comes back unchanged, so hosts that already publish absolute URIs — including VS Code's own — behave exactly as before. The new behaviour applies only to templates that were previously unusable.

## Validation

- `npm run typecheck-client`, `npm run valid-layers-check`, `eslint` on all four files
- `./scripts/test.sh --glob "**/vs/{sessions,workbench/contrib/chat,platform/agentHost}/**/*.test.js"` — 14,495 passing
- Unit tests for the helper: relative joins, fully-qualified passthrough, and separator handling
- An end-to-end test asserts the provider subscribes to `<session>/changeset/uncommitted` and **not** to `file:///changeset/uncommitted`

Verified against the bug by reverting the resolution: the end-to-end test then fails with `verbatim: 1, resolved: undefined`, reproducing the production trace exactly rather than merely failing.

Fixes #332635

`EditorGroupModel.deserialize` decrements the serialized sticky index once per editor that fails to deserialize, but compares each raw index against the already-decremented value. After the first dead sticky slot is processed, later dead slots inside the original sticky range no longer match and are skipped, so a restored group keeps phantom sticky editors (and can keep one on an otherwise empty group). The fix captures the incoming index before the loop and compares against that, so every dead slot within the serialized sticky prefix decrements exactly once. A result of `-1` (all sticky editors dead) is the existing no-sticky sentinel.

title: agentHost: apply customization changes made before the first message
body:
Customization changes made in a draft (not yet sent) session did not reach the agent. This is most
visible for a standalone MCP server, where disabling it appeared to do nothing.

A standalone MCP server is bundled by the client into a synthetic plugin, so the client owns its
global enablement and the host only learns about a change when the client republishes. A draft
session read its customization scope one time, when it created the backend session, and never
again, so nothing was republished. Started sessions were already correct, because the session
handler reconciles them.

Three commits:

**1. Make customization scope acquisition infallible.** `acquireScope` returned `undefined` when no
agent registration existed, which silently degraded a session to no customizations at all. Scopes
are now created on demand and the registration step is deleted, so every caller gets a scope and
the branches that handled an absent one are gone. The user storage option is derived from the
session type instead of passed in.

**2. Republish customizations from a draft session.** Adds a publisher that watches the scope and
sends `SessionActiveClientSet` when it changes. It holds back while the scope is unresolved,
compares against the live session state and the last value sent, and stops when the draft
graduates so it cannot race the session handler.

**3. Read MCP servers and toggles from a draft session.** `getMcpServers` and
`setCustomizationEnablement` looked the session up in the session cache, which a draft does not
enter until it graduates. Both now fall back to the open drafts. Before this, a draft showed the
VS Code actions rather than the agent host ones, and the VS Code workspace action writes to a
different scope than the agent host uses, so the row greyed while the agent kept the server.

Verified with `typecheck-client`, `valid-layers-check`, and the `AgentHost` unit tests. Each new
test was confirmed to fail without its fix.

Two known gaps, both pre-existing and left for follow up: `getFeedbackAnnotationsChannel` looks up
the session cache in the same way and is still draft blind, and an unknown session type now
receives a new scope rather than `undefined`, which removes the last signal that a session type
string does not match a registered harness.

Fixes https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/332257
Fixes https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/332258

body:

Fixes #332631

The async `QueryGlobTester.includedInQuery` disagreed with its sync twin `includedInQuerySync`: it ORed per-expression verdicts so one non-matching exclude overrode an exclusion produced by another expression, and synchronous exclude matches were dropped entirely because the non-thenable branch never consulted the verdict. With several distinct exclude expressions per folder (one plain, one `when` sibling clause), a path excluded by the first could still be reported as included.

The method now applies the same semantics as `includedInQuerySync`: every parsed exclude expression is evaluated once, any synchronous match excludes immediately via a flag, thenables are collected, and if any exist `Promise.all` decides with any-exclude-wins before falling back to the include expression. When nothing is asynchronous the common case returns a plain boolean instead of an already-resolved promise, which matches the method's documented contract; the sole caller (`textSearchManager`) already handles both return forms.

Draft until #332631 receives triage.

- the parsed-expression type domain (`string | null | Promise<string | null>`) was audited to confirm the synchronous detection is exhaustive

title: Touch: forget cancelled touches in the gesture handler
body:
<!-- Thank you for submitting a Pull Request. Please:
* Read our Pull Request guidelines:
  https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/wiki/How-to-Contribute#pull-requests
* Associate an issue with the Pull Request.
* Ensure that the code is up-to-date with the `main` branch.
* Include a description of the proposed changes and how to test them.
-->

Fixes #332619

The `Gesture` singleton listens for `touchstart`, `touchmove` and `touchend` but never for `touchcancel`. When the UA takes a touch over (system gesture, palm rejection, navigation) it delivers `touchcancel`, `onTouchEnd` never runs, and the entry in `activeTouches` stays forever: the DOM node reference is pinned, the target bookkeeping on the node is never undone, and with one stale entry left the single-finger inertia branch treats every session as multi-touch, so inertia scrolling dies after a few cancelled swipes.

Cancelled touches now end the gesture like a normal touchend would: consumers such as the minimap and the sash release their gesture state on the end event, so cancellation dispatches that end event instead of leaving them stuck between start and end. No tap, no context menu and no inertia dispatch is generated for an interrupted gesture. Known limits, unchanged by this fix: iOS Safari sometimes delivers plain `touchend` instead of cancelling, and a `pointercancel` cannot be handled by a touch-events-only consumer.

Draft until #332619 receives triage.

Update: follow-up commit 64dd22694fdb makes cancelled touches dispatch the end gesture event so consumers release their state (see review discussion below); verification harness extended accordingly.

## How was this tested

No touch event harness exists upstream today (prior fixes in this file merged without tests for the same reason), so verification executed the compiled handler directly:

- synthesized `touchcancel` sequences against old and new builds: before the change the cancelled identifier stayed in the internal map; after the change it is removed
- 16/16 behavior vectors verified dynamically, including known-identifier removal, unknown-identifier tolerance (no throw), untouched state of other active touches, and recovery of the single-finger inertia gate once cancels bring the count back to one

body:

Fixes #332616

`sharedMutationObserver.observe` shares one `MutationObserver` per target and options hash and counts users. Only the creating consumer registered the cleanup disposable that decrements the count and disconnects the observer; a second consumer joining later only incremented `users` with no cleanup of its own. Now every observing consumer holds its own cleanup, and the shared event emitter lives on the shared record so it is disposed exactly once regardless of which consumer disposes first.

title: Do not cache a session-state subscription that failed to subscribe
body:
Pinning a visible session is deliberately idempotent, and the code says why:

```ts
// Pin visible sessions… All operations are idempotent, so re-running per tick
// also recovers a subscription that could not be created earlier (e.g. a remote
// provider that was momentarily disconnected).
for (const sessionId of nowVisible) {
    this._ensureSessionStateSubscription(sessionId);
```

That recovery never ran. A subscribe that **failed** was stored in `_sessionStateSubscriptions` exactly like a successful one, so every later tick hit the early return and turned the recovery away.

It is easy to miss because a failed subscribe settles via `onDidError` and never fires `onDidChange` — the only event this consumer listens to. So the session stopped receiving state silently and permanently, with nothing logged.

## How it surfaces

A cloud sandbox addresses a session by the id Mission Control minted, which is issued **before** the host materializes the session. From a trace of one session:

```
34.482  subscribe ahp-session:/8f254d26…   ← the summary subscription
34.571     ← NotFound
35.207  createSession                       ← session now exists
36.550  subscribe → OK, changesets: 6       ← a different consumer, works fine
```

The session summary subscription lost the race by ~700ms and never recovered, so `SessionState.changesets` never reached the adapter. `createChangesets` was therefore never called, no changeset objects existed, and the Changes view stayed on "No Changed Files" for the rest of the session — with no error anywhere.

The same hole applies to the momentarily-disconnected remote the existing comment already describes.

## The fix

Drop the subscription when it errors, covering both orderings:

- if it already carries an error, bail without caching (`onDidError` will not fire again)
- if the error arrives later, delete the entry, guarded on the stored store still being ours so a concurrent re-subscribe is not clobbered

The next tick then re-subscribes, by which point the session exists. No new API, no retry loop, no timers — it just stops defeating the recovery that was already there.

## Why not cache the failure instead

The platform layer already made this call. `AgentSubscriptionManager.getSubscription` evicts an errored entry rather than handing it back:

```ts
if (existing.sub.value instanceof Error) {
    // Failed subscriptions should not poison the resource forever. Evict
    // the errored entry so this acquire performs a fresh subscribe.
```

So this PR does not introduce a retry policy — it stops this consumer from silently opting out of the one that already exists.

Re-acquiring does mean a fresh wire subscribe, so a permanently-failing session retries. That is bounded:

- nothing is on a timer — the pin loop is reactive on `visibleSessions`, and the other caller runs off query paths, so retries are paced by user activity
- the main permanent case self-limits: a session the host stops listing is evicted from `_sessionCache`, and this method then bails at `if (!cached) return;` before subscribing
- eviction is clean — `_disposeSubscriptionEntry` disposes the subscription and sends `unsubscribe`

If a host ever fails the same subscribe indefinitely while still listing the session, the right place for backoff is `getSubscription` — one policy, every consumer — rather than a second, divergent one here. Two layers disagreeing about failed subscriptions is what produced this bug.

## Risk

The changed path only runs when a subscription errors, which today means the session receives nothing at all. A successful subscribe behaves exactly as before.

## Validation

- `npm run typecheck-client`, `npm run valid-layers-check`, `eslint` on both files
- `./scripts/test.sh --glob "**/vs/{sessions,workbench/contrib/chat,platform/agentHost}/**/*.test.js"` — 14,492 passing
- New test drives the real ordering: the first subscribe fails the way a not-yet-created session does, then the host creates it. Asserts the re-subscribe happens **and** that changesets reach the session.

Verified against the bug by reverting the fix and confirming the test fails on the subscribe count (`afterRetry: 1` instead of `2`), so it is pinned to the recovery rather than to the assertion shape.

## Not fixed here

The chat summary can still read `1 file changed +0 -0`. That is a separate defect in the host: `diff_stats` reports a net line-count delta rather than a diff, so any edit preserving line count reports zero. Tracked upstream in `github/copilot-host#860`. Once this PR lands the Changes view defaults to Branch Changes, which uses real `git numstat` and shows correct counts.

title: Avoid unbounded Event.buffer growth on the localPty channel (main process OOM)
body:
Fixes #332603

`ProxyChannel.fromService` eagerly wraps every event of the proxied service in `Event.buffer`. On the `localPty` channel this means the main process buffers **every `onProcessData` event of every terminal for the whole session**: renderers connect to the pty host directly (MessagePort) and never call `listen('onProcessData')` on this channel, so the buffer never gets a listener, never flushes, and grows until the main process hits the ~4 GiB V8 heap cage and aborts (SIGTRAP, no error dialog, all windows lost).

Evidence in #332603: heap snapshot taken at OOM (`--heap-snapshot-on-oom`) shows 285 521 `{ id, event }` objects (3.69 GB of ANSI terminal frames) retained by a single `Event.buffer` array whose source is `PtyHostService.onProcessData`.

This PR passes the already-existing `unbufferedEvents` option to `ProxyChannel.fromService` for the two high-volume terminal events (`onProcessData`, `onProcessReplay`), so they are forwarded only to actual subscribers instead of being buffered forever.

Verified locally by applying the equivalent change to the built `out/main.js` of 1.134.0 — VS Code starts and terminals work normally; the main process no longer accumulates terminal data.

title: chat: explain why Agent Merge turned itself off
body:
Agent Merge could stop monitoring a session without saying anything. The controller only wrote an `info` log line, so from the UI the feature just silently switched itself off.

This is easy to hit on a session using `folder` isolation. The controller pins the branch that was checked out when it was enabled, and any later `git checkout` in that shared clone — from you or from another session — trips the branch-changed guard:

```ts
if (target.branchName !== branchName) {
    this._disable(session, agentMerge, `branch changed from ${target.branchName} to ${branchName}`);
}
```

I found this while investigating a real session where Agent Merge was enabled but never ran. Its persisted config was `{"enabled": false}` with an empty controller state — the signature of a self-disable — and the session's git state had drifted to a completely unrelated branch and pull request. A parallel worktree-isolated session on the same day worked fine and got two repair turns.

## What changes

Both transitions are now reported in the session transcript:

| State | Notice |
|---|---|
| Enabled | Agent Merge is on and watching `<branch>`. |
| Self-disabled | Agent Merge was turned off because the checked-out branch changed from `<a>` to `<b>`. |
| User-disabled | Agent Merge was turned off for this session. |

Rendered as a `systemNotification` part, the same neutral inline treatment as the existing "Created isolated worktree" line.

## Notes for reviewers

**The notice never reaches the agent.** It is dispatched with `dispatchServerAction` only; `AgentSideEffects.handleAction` — the path that forwards a turn to the provider — is deliberately not called. A test asserts `sentToAgent: 0`.

**It needs its own turn.** The chat reducer drops a `ChatResponsePart` whose `turnId` is not the active turn, and disables always happen with no active turn (`_evaluate` early-returns when one is running). So the notice appends to the active turn when there is one, and otherwise synthesizes a start → part → complete turn whose *message* is hidden via `withMessageHiddenFromTranscript`, leaving only the notice visible.

**It survives reload.** Host-injected turns are absent from the SDK transcript replayed on restore, so the notice is recorded through `AgentHostLocalTurns`, the existing mechanism for `!command` and `/rename` turns.

**Reported once.** `_disable()` writes config, which synchronously re-enters `_doSyncSession`. It claims the transition before that write, so the reasoned notice wins and the generic one only fires for user-initiated disables.

**Logs are unchanged.** All ten disable reasons now pair a stable English `log` detail with a localized `notice`, so log-based debugging still works byte-for-byte.

**Not a chat contribution.** The trigger is a host-side config change and matches none of the four `IAgentHostChatContribution` hooks; it follows the existing `startTurn`/`cancelTurn` callback pattern the controller already owns.

## Drive-by fix

`.progress-container` used `align-items: center`, which floated the icon to the vertical middle of a wrapped message. It now sits on the first line. This also affects tool progress rows, which had the same latent bug:

Before — icon centered across three lines; after — icon on line one.

The icon box is sized with `line-height: inherit` so it is exactly one text line tall and stays correct at any font size (measured within 0.21px of the first line's centre).

Writing the fixtures also caught that `ChatSystemNotificationContentPart` hard-coded `Codicon.check`, so "Agent Merge was turned off…" would have rendered with a green checkmark. The icon is now part of `IChatSystemNotificationPart`, defaulting to the existing check so all current callers are unchanged.

## Validation

`typecheck-client` and `valid-layers-check` clean. 30 Agent Merge tests plus the chat rendering suites pass, including new tests for the notice payload, the once-only reporting, and the icon mapping (with a fallback for unrecognized kinds). 12 component fixtures added and verified in the component explorer in both themes.

## Follow-up, not in scope

This makes the failure legible but does not remove the trap: Agent Merge on a shared folder-isolation checkout is still killable by any unrelated `git checkout`. Warning at enable time for `isolation: folder` sessions would be the real fix.

title: Activate Python environments in Agent Host shell commands with shell init scripts
body:
Resolves: https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/332046
Part of: https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/323164

- Generate one init script per Agent Host Copilot session and register it through the SDK's `shell.initScripts`, so it runs before every built-in shell command.
- Source `~/.bashrc` on macOS and Linux, or the current-user PowerShell profiles on Windows, then run the activation command the Python Environments extension published for the session's folder, reading only that extension's value for the tool shell.
- Gate on the default-off, application-scoped `chat.agentHost.shellTool.initScript.enabled` setting and forward it to the host as the `enableShellInitScript` root flag; the host applies a script only while the flag is true and the SDK shell is in use, and unregisters when either changes.
- Publish only from the Editor Window that owns the session folder; any local window may clear. Keep the value transient and session-only, accept at most one entry of 64 KiB, and reconcile synchronously before each turn.
- Materialize one file per session instance, grant its directory to the SDK sandbox before registration, rewrite in place on change, and delete on dispose once the SDK disconnect settles. Failures are logged and retried on the next turn.
- Encode PowerShell activation as base64 and load each profile under `Continue` in its own try/catch.

Notes:

- The forwarded flag is client-writable root config like every forwarded key. Connected Agent Host clients are trusted and can already run commands, so the setting is the user's opt-in mirrored to the host, not authorization.
- With the SDK sandbox enabled, profile files and activation scripts outside the working directory need `allowRead` entries; profile setup repeats before every shell command; direct script commands may need approval while a script is registered (github/copilot-sdk#2466); the Windows E2E variant is skipped by the Copilot output oracle.

title: agent host: anchor side chat forks at the last completed turn
body:
A side chat can branch from a turn that is still running. The host asked the provider to
fork at that active turn, but an active turn is not yet in any provider history. Each
provider then used a different fallback: Copilot inherited all turns, Claude created a
fresh chat, and Codex made an error. Side chats were thus not available for Codex.

The host now anchors the fork at the last completed non-local turn, and the side chat
contribution adds only the turns that the fork cannot carry. Thus the side chat shows the
source conversation one time.

- Adds `resolveLastNonLocalTurnId` to the shared conversation context module. The host and
  the side chat contribution use the same helper, because the two values must agree.
- Anchors an active-turn side chat fork at the last completed non-local turn. The origin
  keeps the identifier of the turn that the user branched from.
- Removes the fork when no completed non-local turn is available, which makes a fresh chat.
  Turn execution uses per-chat queues, thus creation does not wait for the source turn.
- Limits the added context for an active turn to the trailing local turns, the active turn
  message, and the partial response.
- Enables side chats for Codex. No other Codex change is necessary.
- Divides the advertised side chat capability from the end-to-end replay coverage with
  `supportsSideChatsE2E`, which obeys the `supportsChatForkE2E` pattern. The Codex scenario
  stays disabled until focused captures are available.

title: Back off GitHub requests instead of hammering a failing service
body:
## The bug

`GitHubCredentialService` kept no memory of failure. Any failed identity resolution cleared the current generation, so the very next `getCredential()` immediately reissued `GET /user`.

A 401 amplified that. `handleRequestError` invalidates the generation, and both `PullRequestResourceService` and `GitHubQueryService` answer the resulting `onDidInvalidate` by rescheduling **every** fragment and entity at `now` — each of which asks for a credential again. So when `/user` succeeded but real requests kept being refused (an auth outage, or a token GraphQL rejects), this was an unbounded zero-delay loop: roughly one identity request plus nine fragment requests per network round trip, per subscribed pull request, per user, for the whole outage.

The main consumer is `AgentMergeController`, which holds a background pull request subscription per session.

## The fix

New `githubBackoff.ts` holds the concern in one place:

- `GitHubBackoffPolicy` — `{ immediateRetries, base, maximum, jitter, decay? }`
- `gitHubBackoffDelay(policy, scheduler, attempts, minimum?)` — the shared escalating, jittered delay
- `GitHubBackoffGate` — holds back attempts against a subject that keeps failing

Callers **wait** rather than being rejected, so recovery stays automatic once GitHub returns and everyone queued behind one delay shares the single attempt that follows it. Waiters are woken when the record changes instead of sleeping out a stale window, and a caller whose token was replaced mid-wait abandons rather than aborting the replacement''s in-flight request.

A successful `/user` deliberately does **not** clear the record — it only proves identity resolution recovered, and clearing it would reset the delay to zero every round in exactly the loop above. Recovery is signalled by a new token, a new host, or the record decaying (5 min) while nothing fails.

## Also

- **Unified three other escalating retries** onto the same helper: the query service (which previously retried failures at its *normal* poll cadence forever), the capability probe, and `PullRequestResourceService`, which already had an identical inline copy of the formula.
- **Capability probe negative cache** — an unusable probe result was re-probed on *every* capability lookup, and because the fragments that ask still succeed on REST fallbacks nothing throttled it. A degraded result is now reused for an escalating window.

title: Clip the notebook editor to the rounded editor card
body:
With `workbench.experimental.modernUI` enabled the editor part is drawn as a rounded card. A notebook paints square corners on top of it, while a text editor in the same place looks correct.

Notebook editors are not children of the editor part. The widget is parented to a host on the workbench that `OverlayLayoutElement` anchors over the part and clips with `clip-path: content-box`. That host carries no radius, so the clip is a sharp rectangle and `notebook.editorBackground` covers the card corners. Text editors sit inside the part and are clipped by it, which is why only notebooks show this.

Rounding the host makes its content box a rounded rect, so the existing clip follows the card. The widget tags the host with a marker class and keeps the outer edge classes in sync from the part, the same way `OverlayWebview` drives its rules in `floatingPanels.css`, so compact mode is covered as well.

Because the host spans the whole part rather than a single group, this stays correct when the editor is split. A group only loses a corner where it actually meets a corner of the card, and a group in the middle keeps all four square.

title: Round notebook cell surfaces to match the cell outline
body:
Notebook cells draw a rounded outline on `.cell-editor-part::before`, but the surfaces inside it paint square corners, so those corners show past the outline.

Three surfaces are involved. The editor root fills `editor.background` and is `overflow: visible`. Its `.overflow-guard` already clips but carries no radius. The status bar closes the bottom. Because `notebook.cellEditorBackground` differs from `notebook.editorBackground` by design, the square corners are visible on the stock themes too, `#181818` against `#1F1F1F` in Dark Modern.

Matching the radius on each surface is enough on its own, since a background is always clipped to its own border radius.

The rules use child combinators so they only reach the cell's own editor. A descendant selector would also match an editor nested inside the cell, such as a Peek Definition preview, and would give that one the cell radius.

Putting the radius on `.cell-editor-part` together with `overflow: hidden` is not an option instead. The execution progress bar is a child of the part positioned at `top: -3px`, above it, and would be clipped away.

No experimental setting is needed to reproduce this. The rounded cell outline is not behind a flag.

title: Fix false-positive CompletionItem.command deprecation report
body:
Fixes #237861

## Problem

The built-in typescript-language-features extension sets `CompletionItem.command` once, up front, in `provideCompletionItems` (`extensions/typescript-language-features/src/languageFeatures/completions.ts`) and never touches it again in `resolveCompletionItem`. Despite that, resolving a completion item reliably reports `CompletionItem.command` as deprecated ("extension MAY NOT change 'command' of a CompletionItem during resolve"), which is what #237861 asks to fix.

The command is never actually changed. The false positive comes from `CompletionsAdapter.resolveCompletionItem` in `extHostLanguageFeatures.ts`, which converts the item to a wire DTO before and after calling the provider's `resolveCompletionItem`, then diffs `commandIdent`/`commandId`/`commandArguments` on the two DTOs. `CommandsConverter#toInternal` mints a brand new `$ident` on every single conversion for any command with non-empty `arguments` (no memoization keyed on the command object), so `commandIdent` differs across the two conversions even when the underlying `vscode.Command` never changed. Any provider that sets `command` with arguments and also implements `resolveCompletionItem` gets flagged unconditionally.

This dto-based diff was introduced in #186179 ("improve deprecated API reporting"), which replaced an earlier, correct check that compared the raw `vscode.Command` objects directly.

Note that `typescript-language-features` sets `command.arguments` to `[item]` specifically to work around VS Code sometimes applying a completion before `resolveCompletionItem` finishes (#109439) — auto-imports would otherwise be silently dropped on fast accepts. So the fix isn't in the extension; it can't stop passing arguments without regressing that fix.

## Fix

Compare the actual `vscode.Command` objects (captured before and after invoking the provider) instead of the converted DTOs. This is close to the pre-#186179 behavior, with one improvement: the "before" command is snapshotted prior to calling the provider, so an in-place mutation of the same item's `command` is still caught (comparing dto/command only after resolve would miss that case, since resolved and original would be the same object by the time it's read).

## Testing

Added a unit test in `src/vs/workbench/api/test/browser/extHostLanguageFeatures.test.ts` that registers a completion provider whose `command` mirrors the ts/js extension's shape (set once at provide time, argument is the item itself, left untouched in `resolveCompletionItem`), resolves the item, and asserts no `CompletionItem.command` deprecation is reported. The test follows the existing `CodeLens, do not resolve a resolved lens` pattern in the same file, and fails against the pre-fix code (traced manually: the old ident-diff always disagrees across the two conversions).

I was not able to run this test or typecheck the change in my environment — there's no `node_modules` installed and a full install was out of scope for this change. I've traced the RPC call path (`ExtHostLanguageFeatures.$resolveCompletionItem` → `MainThreadLanguageFeatures`'s registered provider → `CompletionItem.resolve` in `editor/contrib/suggest`) by hand to confirm the test exercises the real code path, but this hasn't been machine-verified.

title: Scroll hover widget when dragging selection past its edge
body:
Fixes #239704

## Problem

Starting a text selection with the mouse inside the hover widget and dragging past its top/bottom edge does nothing useful: the content doesn't scroll and the hover disappears.

The disappearing part turned out to be the more interesting bug. `ContentHoverController._onEditorMouseMove` hides the hover while dragging (`this._isMouseDown && !this._shouldKeepHoverWidgetVisible(...)`), and the comment right above it says this is meant for drags that *started outside* the hover widget so the widget doesn't cover a selection made in the editor text. But the check never actually looked at where the mousedown happened — only where the mouse currently is — so a selection that starts inside the hover and drags past its edge hits the same "hide" path.

Separately, even with the hover staying open, there was no way to scroll it: `HoverWidget`'s scrollable content uses `overflow: hidden` (Monaco's usual custom-scrollbar approach), which also disables the browser's native drag-to-autoscroll for text selection.

## Fix

- `contentHoverController.ts`: track whether the mousedown that's currently held started on the content hover widget (`_isMouseDownOnContentHoverWidget`). If it did, dragging outside the widget's bounds keeps it open instead of hiding/recomputing it.
- `hoverWidget.ts` (`src/vs/base/browser/ui/hover/hoverWidget.ts`): while a selection drag is active, auto-scroll the content when the mouse crosses near the top/bottom edge, with scroll speed proportional to how far past the edge the mouse is. This follows the same shape as `listView.ts`'s existing DND autoscroll (`animateDragAndDropScrollTop`), using `dom.animate` to drive the loop each frame and clamping handled by `ScrollState`, the same as the existing `scrollUp`/`scrollDown` methods on `ContentHoverWidget`.

This lives on the shared `HoverWidget` base class (which owns `contentsDomNode`/`scrollbar`), so it applies to both the editor content/glyph hovers and the generic workbench hover built on top of it, not just the editor content hover.

Known limitation: the scroll is driven by `mousemove`, so if you drag past the edge and then hold the mouse still, the content keeps scrolling but the selection itself won't keep extending until the mouse moves again (same as it currently behaves once the drag re-enters the hover). Making the selection extend on a stationary mouse would need synthetic mousemove dispatch or `caretRangeFromPoint`/`selection.extend()`, which felt out of scope for this fix.

## Testing

Typechecked both changed files directly (`tsc --noEmit`) — the only diagnostics were pre-existing `*.css` side-effect-import errors that show up for any file in this checkout since there's no `node_modules`/build step here, unrelated to this change.

There's no existing test under `src/vs/editor/contrib/hover/test` that exercises mouse drag/selection, and jsdom doesn't produce real layout (`scrollHeight`, `getBoundingClientRect`), so there wasn't a meaningful unit test to add for the scroll math itself. I was not able to manually verify the drag interaction in a running build in this environment — the fix is based on reading the mouse-hide logic and the existing drag-to-scroll pattern in `listView.ts`.

title: Load ESM extensions synchronously so codeLoadingTime is accurate
body:
Fixes #332556

### The problem

`codeLoadingTime` for an ESM extension could include time spent loading *other* extensions.

The module itself isn't slow — its evaluation is already serialised by Node. What's slow is the `await`. When several extensions activate together they all start their timer at once, and the one that finishes first still can't resume until whoever is evaluating gives the thread back. Measured on a trivial module loading next to a 300ms one:

```
actual evaluation timeline (from inside the modules):
    eval:probe        0ms      <- evaluated instantly
    eval:burn:start   0ms
    eval:burn:end   300ms

what the timer saw:
    probe   started 0ms  settled 300ms  -> reported 300ms
```

The number isn't only used for telemetry — it also drives the "slow extension" warnings in the Running Extensions editor and the extension hover, so ESM extensions could be blamed for their neighbours' startup cost.

### The fix

Load ESM extensions with Node's synchronous `require(esm)` path, the same one Node uses when CJS code requires an ESM module. Nothing else can run during a synchronous load, so the timer covers that extension's own work by construction.

ESM modules using top-level `await` can't be loaded synchronously. Node reports those with `ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE` *before evaluating anything*, so those fall back to `import()` with nothing half-loaded behind them. `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` falls back the same way, so a runtime without `require(esm)` keeps working.

This also moves the localization setup out of the timed section. It was sitting inside the measurement and inflating the number for CJS extensions too.

### Numbers

40 ESM extensions activating together, a third of them doing ~40ms of real work:

| | total | reported median | max |
|---|---|---|---|
| `import()` (today) | 651ms | 609ms | 650ms |
| `require(esm)` | 632ms | 2ms | 43ms |

Accurate, and not slower.

### What extensions using top-level await get

Both attempts are timed as one span, because the failed `require` is what parses the module graph — usually most of the cost — and `import()` then reuses it from cache. That parsing is measured exactly, since it's synchronous. Only whatever runs after the `await` resumes is wall clock and can still pick up other extensions' work.

So these extensions get a partly accurate number rather than no benefit. Timing both attempts matters: timing only the `import()` reports roughly zero for them, which would quietly hide a genuinely expensive extension.

### Notes for whoever reads the telemetry

- `codeLoadingTime` keeps its name but now means "what this extension cost" rather than "how long until it was ready". Values will step down, correctly, so dashboards trending it across the release will show a discontinuity.
- The "how long until it was ready" view isn't lost: the `willLoadExtensionCode` / `didLoadExtensionCode` perf marks still cover the whole wait and already ship via `startup.timer.mark`. No new telemetry fields.
- `activateCallTime` brackets a synchronous call and was never affected by any of this. `activateResolvedTime` waits on the extension's own promise and still includes whatever else runs during that wait — untouched here. Both "slow extension" UI surfaces sum `codeLoadingTime + activateCallTime` and leave `activateResolvedTime` out, so they're now correct.

### One behaviour change worth knowing about

For a module with a `default` export, `require(esm)` adds an `__esModule: true` marker to the namespace that `import()` doesn't:

| module | `require(esm)` | `import()` |
|---|---|---|
| only named exports | `[activate, deactivate]` | `[activate, deactivate]` |
| has a default export | `[__esModule, activate, default]` | `[activate, default]` |

`activate` and `deactivate` are identical either way, so activation itself is unaffected. It's only visible when an extension has no `activate` function, because then the module namespace is handed out as that extension's `exports` — a consumer doing `__esModule ? mod.default : mod` interop would start unwrapping `.default`. Narrow, but it is a public API surface change.

### Verified

`require(esm)` keeps working with the ext host's `registerHooks` interception for the `vscode` bare specifier (including the `data:` URL API instances), returns the same module namespace object as `import()` with live bindings intact, and preserves `import.meta.url` / `resolve` / `dirname` and module-evaluation error shapes. Builtin imports, JSON import attributes, `createRequire`, ESM↔CJS interop, circular imports and `"type": "module"` entry points all load synchronously; only top-level `await` falls back.

Worth exercising in CI on all three platforms for extensions loaded out of an `.asar`.

title: fix: wrap Luna dictation alias picker endpoint in test mock (build fix for vscode-engineering#3637)
body:
## Build failure

The unit test `LanguageModelAccess model info › publishes a core-only Luna alias for dictation cleanup without publishing hidden models directly` failed on `main`. It asserts `lunaPublishedDirectly: false` but observed `true`, so the hidden `gpt-5.6-luna` model was being published as a top-level, user-selectable language model.

## Root cause

The failure is a test-setup regression, not a production defect. In production, `AutomodeService.resolveAutoModePickerEndpoint` (`extensions/copilot/src/platform/endpoint/node/automodeService.ts`) always wraps the chosen base endpoint in an `AutoChatEndpoint`, which is published under the pseudo model id `auto`. A hidden model such as `gpt-5.6-luna` is therefore never surfaced directly in the model picker.

The test's `IAutomodeService` mock instead returned the raw `lunaEndpoint` from `resolveAutoModePickerEndpoint`. `LanguageModelAccess._provideLanguageModelChatInfo` then pushed that hidden endpoint into the published set under its own model id `gpt-5.6-luna`, making `lunaPublishedDirectly` true. The assertion was correct; the mock was infidelitous to production behavior.

## How the fix works

The mock now mirrors production by returning a real `AutoChatEndpoint` that wraps `lunaEndpoint`. The wrapper is instantiated from the test's instantiation service (all required services — `IDomainService`, `ICAPIClientService`, etc. — are provided by `createExtensionTestingServices`) after the testing accessor is created, and assigned to the closure variable the mock returns. A base-count cache entry for the `auto` pseudo model is pre-seeded (matching the existing pattern for the other endpoints) to keep the test deterministic and fast. With the wrapper in place, the picker endpoint publishes as `auto`, `gpt-5.6-luna` is no longer published directly, and the assertion passes.

## Rollback evaluation

Recommendation: **Do not roll back**.

Public culprit commit/PR: `83dfbdd3a9d94908ae3c92c3ec0ca34f2afe8dcf` (PR #331338). The originating change is a legitimate feature (a core-only Luna dictation-cleanup alias); only its accompanying test mock diverged from production behavior. A fix-forward on the test is bounded and safer than reverting the feature. Owners to consult: `@meganrogge`.

## Validation

Automated validation (typecheck/test) could not be run in this environment because Node.js execution is blocked. The change was verified by source inspection against `automodeService.resolveAutoModePickerEndpoint`, `AutoChatEndpoint`, and `LanguageModelAccess._provideLanguageModelChatInfo`, confirming the mock now matches the production wrapping contract.

## Risk

Low. The change is confined to a single test file's mock setup and does not touch production code.

## Recommended reviewer

Recommended owner: `@meganrogge`

title: snap: stage libpulse0 so Chromium can use PulseAudio/PipeWire
body:
snap: stage `libpulse0` so Chromium can use PulseAudio/PipeWire

## Problem

Microphone capture does not work in the `code` snap on Linux. Speech-to-text
(`ms-vscode.vscode-speech`) fails with:

> Could not access the microphone for speech-to-text: Could not start audio source

The same failure affects anything that calls `getUserMedia()` in the snap.
Reproduced on Ubuntu 26.04 with VS Code 1.134.0 (snap rev 258), PipeWire 1.6.2
and `pipewire-pulse`. The microphone itself is fine — `pw-record` against the
default source captures audio normally, and Chrome (`.deb`) records without
issue on the same machine.

## Root cause

`resources/linux/snap/snapcraft.yaml` stages `libasound2` but not `libpulse0`,
and `core20` does not ship libpulse either:

```
$ ls /snap/core20/current/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/ | grep pulse
(nothing)
$ find /snap/code/258 -name 'libpulse*'
(nothing)
```

Chromium `dlopen()`s `libpulse.so.0` to select its PulseAudio backend. When that
fails it silently falls back to the ALSA backend. The snap's ALSA then has no
way to reach the sound server: the host routes the `default` device through
`libasound_module_pcm_pipewire.so`, and the snap runtime contains no
`alsa-lib/` plugin directory at all. Opening a capture device therefore fails,
surfacing as *"Could not start audio source"*.

The difference is visible by comparing the audio service of a working app with
the snap's:

```
# Chrome (.deb) — microphone works
$ grep -oE '/\S*lib(pulse|asound)\S*' /proc/$CHROME_AUDIO_PID/maps | sort -u
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libasound.so.2.0.0
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libpulse.so.0.24.3
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/pulseaudio/libpulsecommon-17.0.so

# code snap — microphone fails
$ grep -oE '/\S*lib(pulse|asound)\S*' /proc/$CODE_AUDIO_PID/maps | sort -u
/snap/code/258/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libasound.so.2.0.0
```

No libpulse is mapped in the snap — only ALSA.

This is not distro-specific: it applies to any host where the microphone sits
behind PulseAudio or PipeWire, which is the default on current desktop Linux.
Users cannot work around it, because the host's libpulse targets a newer glibc
(2.43 on Ubuntu 26.04) than the `core20` runtime (2.31), so it cannot be
injected via `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`.

## Fix

Add `libpulse0` to `stage-packages`. Snapcraft pulls in the transitive
dependencies that `core20` lacks (`libsndfile1`, `libasyncns0` and their
codec dependencies) and rewrites the `RUNPATH` of the staged libraries for
classic confinement, so `libpulsecommon` resolves inside the snap.

`libpulse0` is not present in `core20`, so the existing `cleanup` part will not
strip it from the prime directory.

## Verification

The `core20` build of libpulse is 13.99.1. To confirm that version can talk to a
current sound server, I extracted the focal `libpulse0` package — exactly what
snapcraft stages for `core20` — and opened a record stream against the host's
`pipewire-pulse` on Ubuntu 26.04:

```
loaded: libpulse-simple.so.0
PASS: connected to PulseAudio server, record stream open
PASS: read 6400 bytes of PCM, peak amplitude = 19

# libraries actually mapped:
/tmp/pulse-shim/lib/libpulse.so.0.21.2
/tmp/pulse-shim/lib/libpulsecommon-13.99.so
/tmp/pulse-shim/lib/libsndfile.so.1.0.28
/tmp/pulse-shim/lib/libasyncns.so.0.3.1
```

The PulseAudio wire protocol is stable, and `pipewire-pulse` serves the older
client without trouble.

I also confirmed the snap runtime can reach the socket, so the library is the
only missing piece:

```
$ echo 'echo $LD_LIBRARY_PATH; ls -d $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/pulse' | snap run --shell code
/tmp/pulse-shim/lib
/run/user/1000/pulse
```

## Risk

Low. One additional stage-package; the snap grows by roughly 1 MB. Behaviour is
unchanged on hosts without a PulseAudio server, where Chromium continues to fall
back to ALSA exactly as it does today.

I could not run a full snap build locally, so it is worth confirming on CI that
snapcraft's classic ELF patching resolves `libpulsecommon-13.99.so` from
`$SNAP/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/pulseaudio/` in the built artefact.

title: Address review feedback on external session files removal
body:
Follow-ups to #332538, which removed external session files from the agent host adaptor. Each item addresses a review comment left on that PR.

### Release per-chat caches when a peer chat is removed

#332538 made per-chat parsing lazy, but the caches backing it — `outputByChat`, `lastTurnChangesByChat` and `customizationsByChat` — had no eviction path. When `_applyChatCatalog` drops a peer, the `AdditionalChat` is disposed, yet those maps retained that chat's observables and parser state for the lifetime of the adapter, so repeated chat creation/deletion leaked one object graph per deleted chat.

`ISessionOutputObs` gains a `releaseChat(chatUri)` method, called from the existing peer-pruning loop in `_applyChatCatalog`. That loop already iterates exactly the chats the catalog no longer lists and is reached before either return path, so it is the single place both removal routes pass through. Keys are protocol chat URIs, so the chat id is mapped back with `buildChatUri`.

### Correct stale API documentation

`IAgentFeedbackService.getSessionForFile` still documented the old behavior — that files outside the session's workspace folders return `undefined`. Since #332538 the only exclusion is output-channel resources, so the doc now says that rather than guiding consumers by obsolete behavior.

### Cover the lazy-subscription contract

The laziness introduced by #332538 was only exercised indirectly through the parser. Three regression tests now pin the actual contract using a recording `IAgentConnection` that tracks acquired and still-open subscription references:

- a chat that is never observed opens no subscription;
- observing one chat subscribes to that chat alone, and disposing the observer releases it;
- `releaseChat` drops the cached observables so a later request rebuilds them.

The first two would have failed under the pre-#332538 fan-out, and the third fails without the eviction fix above.

### Validation

`npm run typecheck-client` clean, and the `agentHostSessionFiles` suite passes with 11 tests including the 3 new ones.

## What & why

Legacy Copilot CLI → Agent Host migration. Makes `chat.agentSessions.migrateLegacyCopilotCli` restart-frozen and fixes several
correctness/UX issues in how sessions hand off between the extension-host and Agent-Host providers. Normal and external sessions are unaffected.

## Changes

- **Setting frozen at startup.** The shared Agent Host survives window reload, so the   setting now applies only after a restart: renderer, extension host, and Agent Host each   read a one-time startup snapshot (via a new `BlockStartup` gate); the old live   enable/disable rediscovery machinery is removed. Setting is `APPLICATION`-scoped and the  relauncher prompts to restart on change.

- **No dropped rows mid-migration.** `AgentSessionsModel` preserves live-registered  (agent-host / remote) provider rows across a sibling's partial refresh. `AgentService`  surfaces an adopted row *before* the slower restore (never absent from both lists) and
  authoritatively refuses unregistered non-adoptable chats. The extension CLI provider  stands down only when the host would actually surface the row (a resumable target  exists), so a dead session is never orphaned; archived legacy sessions stay until opened.

- **Adopt-on-open UX.** The opener and `chatEditorInput` restore run the adopt probe under a  subtle "Opening chat…" progress hint, gated to migrated resources so normal opens stay  overhead-free; open/restore timeout budgets raised for a still-cold host.

- **Archived correctness.** Persisted archived state is rehydrated on item re-emit so an  archived row can't be resurrected; archived legacy sessions migrate on open.

- **Transcript cleanliness.** `mapSessionEvents` strips `<system-reminder>` scaffolding so  derived titles/previews aren't polluted.
